lecture_plan.chapter_arc: We start with a puzzle — why carbon compounds behave so differently from the ionic compounds we already know — and trace it back to a single answer: the covalent bond. From that one idea we build outward: how carbon's bonding makes millions of compounds, how we organize and name them, how they react, and finally how a handful of these molecules — ethanol, ethanoic acid, soaps — shape everyday life.
lecture_plan.opening_hook: Ionic compounds melt at hundreds of degrees and conduct electricity — yet alcohol, vinegar, and the gas in your stove melt low, boil easily, and conduct nothing. What kind of bond hides behind this whole different world of chemistry?

coverage_checklist.description: Explain the covalent bond as electron sharing and why it gives carbon compounds low melting/boiling points and poor conductivity, contrasting with ionic compounds
Show that carbon's tetravalency and catenation (self-linking) are what generate millions of compounds
Distinguish saturated from unsaturated compounds and connect double/triple bonds to reactivity
Introduce functional groups and the homologous series as the organizing order behind carbon chemistry
Teach the IUPAC naming system using carbon chain length plus prefix/suffix for functional groups
Cover the four key reaction types — combustion, oxidation, addition, substitution — and link each to structure (saturated vs unsaturated)
Detail ethanol and ethanoic acid as concrete, important everyday carbon compounds with their properties and uses
Explain how soaps clean by bridging oil and water using a molecule with one water-loving and one oil-loving end

lecture_plan.closing_summary: We opened with a mystery: why alcohol, vinegar, and cooking gas behave nothing like the ionic compounds we knew. The answer was the covalent bond — carbon sharing electrons rather than giving them away. From that single idea everything followed: carbon's four bonds and its love of linking to itself give us millions of compounds, which we tamed with functional groups, homologous series, and naming rules; we saw them burn, oxidize, add, and substitute; and we met the molecules — ethanol, ethanoic acid, and soap — that turn this chemistry into wine, vinegar, and clean clothes. Carbon's quiet covalent bond is the thread running through living things and everyday materials alike.

segments.narration_chapter: Salt melts at over eight hundred degrees, but candle wax melts in your warm hand — both are just atoms stuck together, so why the huge difference? <<SECTION:Carbon compounds are different|id=sec-1>> The wax, like most carbon compounds, has a very low melting point and won't conduct electricity — and those two clues tell us something big. No conduction means there are no ions floating around, so carbon is NOT stealing or donating electrons the way sodium and chlorine do in salt. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:carbon_and_its_compounds:4_1:carbon_shell_diagram>> <<SECTION:Carbon's electron problem|id=sec-2>> To see why, let's look inside a carbon atom: six electrons, <<FOCUS:inner-shell>> two tucked in the inner shell, and <<FOCUS:valence-electrons>> four sitting in the outer shell. <<FOCUS:need-label>> Carbon wants eight in that outer shell to feel stable, and right now it has exactly four — sitting right in the middle. <<UNFOCUS>> So here's the honest question: could carbon just grab four extra electrons, or throw away the four it has, to reach a full shell? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Gaining or losing 4 electrons needs too much energy — impossible|id=key-1>> It can't — pulling in four electrons or ripping four away would take an enormous amount of energy, far more than carbon can manage, so neither happens. <<PAUSE:short>> So carbon does something cleverer: instead of stealing or giving, it SHARES its electrons with other atoms. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:carbon_and_its_compounds:4_1:methane_shared_pairs>> <<SECTION:Sharing pairs|id=sec-3>> Watch <<FOCUS:hydrogen-atoms>> carbon meet four hydrogen atoms — each hydrogen has one electron, and each one <<FOCUS:central-carbon>> pairs up with one of carbon's electrons. Here's the magic of a shared pair: <<FOCUS:shared-pair>> this single pair of electrons is <<FOCUS:shared-pair+central-carbon+hydrogen-atoms>> counted by the carbon AND by the hydrogen at the same time. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Here's an example from the chapter. We're given the melting and boiling points of four carbon compounds, and we want to see what these numbers tell us about the forces holding their molecules together. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: What do the melting and boiling points of carbon compounds reveal about their intermolecular forces?|id=ex-q-1>> Let's lay out the data. Acetic acid melts at two hundred ninety kelvin and boils at three hundred ninety-one kelvin. <<WRITE_STEP:Acetic acid: melts 290 K, boils 391 K|id=ex-step-1-1>> Chloroform melts at two hundred nine kelvin and boils at three hundred thirty-four kelvin. <<WRITE_STEP:Chloroform: melts 209 K, boils 334 K|id=ex-step-1-2>> Ethanol melts at one hundred fifty-six kelvin and boils at three hundred fifty-one kelvin. <<WRITE_STEP:Ethanol: melts 156 K, boils 351 K|id=ex-step-1-3>> And methane melts at just ninety kelvin and boils at one hundred eleven kelvin. <<WRITE_STEP:Methane: melts 90 K, boils 111 K|id=ex-step-1-4>> Notice how low all of these values are when compared to ionic compounds, which often melt at well over a thousand kelvin. Two hydrogen atoms <<FOCUS:shared-pair>> share their electrons, contributing one electron each, to form a molecule of hydrogen, H two. <<WRITE_STEP:Hydrogen, atomic number 1, has 1 electron in K shell and needs 1 more.|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:Two H atoms each share one electron to form H2.|id=ex-step-1-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> By sharing, each hydrogen atom now attains the configuration of the nearest noble gas, helium, which has two electrons in its K shell. What would happen in the case of a diatomic molecule of nitrogen? To do this, each nitrogen atom contributes three electrons. <<WRITE_STEP:Each nitrogen contributes three electrons to attain an octet|id=ex-step-1-1>> Those contributed electrons give rise to three shared pairs of electrons, and three shared pairs constitute a triple bond between the two atoms. Let us take a look at methane, which is a compound of carbon. segments.narration_chapter: Chemists have catalogued millions of different carbon compounds — more than every other element on the entire periodic table makes when you add them all together. <<SECTION:Why carbon?|id=sec-1>> That is a staggering imbalance, so there must be something special about this one little atom. It comes down to the way carbon shares electrons to make covalent bonds. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:carbon_and_its_compounds:4_2:carbon_skeletons>> Here is the trick. A carbon atom can bond not just to other elements, but to other carbon atoms — over and over again. <<PAUSE:short>> Picture carbon atoms linking hands. They can form a <<TRACE:straight-chain>> long straight chain like this, one carbon holding the next, holding the next. <<WRITE_KEY:Catenation = carbon bonding to carbon, in chains, branches and rings|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> But they need not stay in a straight line. A chain can <<FOCUS:branched-chain>> branch off in a new direction, or even curl around and <<FOCUS:carbon-ring>> join up into a ring. <<UNFOCUS>> This linking-up is called catenation. <<PAUSE:short>> And the links themselves can vary — carbon atoms can be joined by single bonds, <<FOCUS:double-bond-link>> or by double bonds, or even triple bonds. <<WRITE_TEXT:chains + branches + rings + bond types = millions|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now think about how many different molecules you can build by mixing chains, branches, rings, and three kinds of bond. That combination explosion is exactly where the millions come from. <<PAUSE:short>> But here is the puzzle — silicon sits right below carbon and also makes four bonds. So why does silicon only manage chains of seven or eight atoms, while carbon goes on almost forever? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:carbon_and_its_compounds:4_2:carbon_bond_count>> <<SECTION:Why carbon and not silicon?|id=sec-2>> The answer is size. <<FOCUS:central-carbon>> Carbon is a tiny atom, so its shared electrons sit very close to both nuclei. With <<FOCUS:four-arms+arm-2+arm-3+arm-4>> four bonding arms and that small size, the bond between two carbon atoms is held together extremely tightly — it is strong and stable. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:silicon-comparison>> Silicon is a bigger atom. Its shared electrons are further from the nuclei, so <<FOCUS:silicon-caption>> silicon-to-silicon bonds are weaker and the chains fall apart quickly. <<UNFOCUS>> So remember this — catenation, carbon's gift for bonding endlessly to itself in chains, branches and rings, is the single biggest reason there are millions of carbon compounds, and its small strong bonds are why carbon, and no other element, pulls it off. <<PAUSE:short>>

Start with the simplest move: link two carbons together <<FOCUS:single-bond>> with a single bond, just one line between them. <<UNFOCUS>> But carbon has a valency of four — it wants four bonds — and right now each carbon has used only one, leaving three empty hands on each. <<WRITE_TEXT:Fill spare bonds with hydrogen|id=text-1>> So we fill every spare bond with a hydrogen — <<FOCUS:hydrogen-set-ethane>> three hydrogens on each carbon — and now every single atom has exactly the bonds it wants. <<WRITE_KEY:Every bond single = saturated = unreactive|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> When every bond between the carbons is a single bond like this, the compound is called saturated, and saturated compounds are normally not very reactive. <<PAUSE:short>> Two carbons joined by a single bond, each carrying three hydrogens, gives a molecule of two carbons and six hydrogens. <<WRITE_EQUATION:C_2H_6|id=eq-1|boxed>> Now here's the puzzle: there is a compound with two carbons but only four hydrogens, not six. Where did those two missing hydrogens go? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> The two carbons couldn't find enough hydrogens, so instead they shared an extra bond between themselves — <<FOCUS:double-bond>> they form a double bond. With that second carbon-to-carbon bond in place, <<FOCUS:hydrogen-set-ethene>> each carbon needs only two hydrogens, which is exactly why this molecule has four hydrogens instead of six. <<UNFOCUS>> Two carbons joined by a double bond, each carrying only two hydrogens, gives a molecule of two carbons and four hydrogens. <<WRITE_EQUATION:C_2H_4|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<FOCUS:double-bond>> Look closely at that double bond — one of those two shared bonds is loosely held, <<FOCUS:spare-bond-marker>> a spare bond just waiting for something to come along. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Here's an example from the chapter. Let's build the structure of ethane, whose formula is two carbons and six hydrogens. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Build the structure of ethane (C2H6)|id=ex-q-1>> The first step is to <<FOCUS:single-bond>> link the two carbon atoms together with a single bond. <<WRITE_STEP:Step 1: join carbon to carbon with a single bond, C—C|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now, each carbon has four valencies. After using one for the carbon-to-carbon bond, three valencies of each carbon atom remain unsatisfied. <<WRITE_STEP:Each carbon has 3 unsatisfied valencies remaining|id=ex-step-1-2>> So we satisfy those by <<FOCUS:hydrogen-set-ethane>> bonding each carbon to three hydrogen atoms. <<WRITE_STEP:Bond each carbon to 3 hydrogen atoms|id=ex-step-1-3>> <<UNFOCUS>> And the structure is complete: two carbons joined by a single bond, each carrying three hydrogens, giving us ethane with two carbons and six hydrogens. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Ethane: H3C—CH3 (C2H6), all valencies satisfied|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. Let's look at propane, whose molecular formula is three carbons and eight hydrogens. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Draw the structure of propane (C3H8) and identify its bonding|id=ex-q-1>> We start by joining the three carbon atoms in a chain, and then we add hydrogen atoms around them. When we draw it out, we find that every single bond is just a single line connecting two atoms, and the valencies of all the atoms are satisfied by single bonds between them. <<WRITE_STEP:Three carbons joined in a chain, each valency completed with single bonds to hydrogen|id=ex-step-1-1>> Since all the valencies here are satisfied entirely by single bonds, such carbon compounds are called saturated compounds. So propane is a saturated compound. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Propane is a saturated compound — all valencies satisfied by single bonds|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. We have a compound of carbon and hydrogen called ethene, whose formula is two carbons and four hydrogens. Let's build its structure using the same step-wise approach. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Draw the structure of ethene (two carbons, four hydrogens)|id=ex-q-1>> We start with step one: we link the two carbon atoms together <<FOCUS:single-bond>> with a single bond between them. <<WRITE_STEP:Step 1: Join the two carbons with a single bond, C - C|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now step two. Each carbon has a valency of four. After the single bond to the other carbon and bonds to its hydrogens, we see that one valency per carbon atom still remains unsatisfied. <<WRITE_STEP:Step 2: One valency per carbon remains unsatisfied|id=ex-step-1-2>> So in step three, this can be satisfied only if there is <<FOCUS:double-bond>> a double bond between the two carbons. <<UNFOCUS>> The two leftover valencies pair up to form that second bond. <<WRITE_STEP:Step 3: Form a double bond between the two carbons, C = C|id=ex-step-1-3>> And the answer is: <<FOCUS:double-bond>> ethene has a double bond between its two carbon atoms, which satisfies all the valencies. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Ethene has a carbon-carbon double bond (C = C) satisfying all valencies|id=ex-ans-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Here's an example from the chapter. We have a compound of hydrogen and carbon called ethyne, whose formula is two carbons and two hydrogens. The question is: how many bonds are necessary between the two carbon atoms to satisfy their valencies? <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Ethyne (two carbons, two hydrogens) — how many bonds between the carbons?|id=ex-q-1>> Let's count. Each carbon has a valency of four. With only two hydrogens to share between two carbons, that's just one hydrogen per carbon, using up one bond each. That leaves three bonds still needed on each carbon, and the only place left to put them is between the two carbons themselves. How many different molecules can you build from exactly these pieces? Most people say one. The answer is two. <<PAUSE:long>> <<SECTION:Carbon chains|id=sec-1>> To see why, start simple. Take three carbons in a row, then attach the fourth not at the end, but <<FOCUS:branched-skeleton>> hanging off the middle one. <<UNFOCUS>> A branch. Fill every spare bond with hydrogen again, and count the atoms. Four carbons. Ten hydrogens. A straight chain and a branched chain are different substances, with different boiling points and behaviour, even sharing one formula. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Rings|id=sec-3>> But carbon has one more trick. segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:carbon_and_its_compounds:4_2_3:chain_swap>> What if you could pluck one hydrogen off a carbon chain, snap something else into its place, and completely change what the molecule does? So far carbon has only made friends with hydrogen, giving us <<FOCUS:carbon-chain+hydrogen-atoms>> those chains and rings we call hydrocarbons. <<SECTION:Carbon makes other friends|id=sec-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> But carbon is a very friendly element, and hydrogen is not its only companion. Carbon also happily bonds with the halogens, which are chlorine, bromine, fluorine, and iodine, and with oxygen, nitrogen, and sulphur. <<WRITE_TEXT:Carbon bonds: halogens, O, N, S too|id=text-1>> Here is the trick. <<FOCUS:target-hydrogen>> Take one hydrogen hanging off the chain, and decide that this is the one we want to swap out. <<UNFOCUS>> Now, if we just yank that hydrogen off, won't carbon be left with a lonely, unsatisfied bond? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Yes, and <<FOCUS:free-valency>> that dangling bond is exactly the opening we need. We call it a free valency, and we fill it by snapping a new partner into place so carbon's bonding capacity of four stays perfectly satisfied. <<UNFOCUS>> The element or group that replaces the hydrogen has a special name. <<WRITE_TEXT:Heteroatom = the atom replacing H|id=text-2>> A single replacing atom, like a chlorine or an oxygen, is called a heteroatom. When that heteroatom comes as part of a recognisable group, attached through that single free valency, <<FOCUS:functional-group>> we call the whole thing a functional group. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So replacing a hydrogen on a carbon chain with a heteroatom or group is what gives you a functional group. <<WRITE_KEY:Swap an H for a group = a functional group|id=key-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> And here is the beautiful part. The functional group decides how the molecule behaves, regardless of whether the carbon chain is short or long, straight or branched. <<PAUSE:short>> Whether you hang an O-H group on a two-carbon chain or a twenty-carbon chain, <<FOCUS:functional-group>> that O-H is what makes both behave like alcohols. <<WRITE_TEXT:Group sets properties, not chain length|id=text-3>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So carbon's friendliness is the whole story here: one swapped hydrogen, one new group, and an entirely new family of compounds with its own personality.

Every one of these has the same little attachment on the end — the alcohol group, <<FOCUS:oh-group-column>> that oxygen-hydrogen pair. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:The functional group rules|id=sec-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> And that attachment is the boss. The functional group, not how long the carbon chain is, decides how the compound reacts. <<PAUSE:short>> So whether the chain behind it is one carbon long or four carbons long, the chemistry stays basically the same. <<WRITE_KEY:Functional group decides the chemistry, not chain length|id=key-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> A family like this — same functional group sitting on <<FOCUS:oh-group-column>> carbon chains of growing length — has a name: a homologous series. <<WRITE_TEXT:Homologous series = same group, growing chain|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now look at how we climb from one rung to the next. Going from methanol up to ethanol, what exactly did we add? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Just one extra carbon and two extra hydrogens — <<FOCUS:ch2-step>> a single CH2 unit. <<UNFOCUS>> And from ethanol to propanol, again one CH2. <<WRITE_TEXT:Each step adds one CH2|id=text-2>> <<SECTION:The CH2 staircase|id=sec-2>> So every member of a homologous series differs from the next <<FOCUS:ch2-step>> by exactly one CH2 unit. <<UNFOCUS>> It's a perfectly regular staircase. <<WRITE_KEY:Successive members differ by one CH2|id=key-2>> <<PAUSE:short>> Because each step adds the same CH2 unit, the molecular mass jumps by the same amount every time — that's a carbon at twelve plus two hydrogens, fourteen units heavier per step. This regularity is exactly why we can write one general formula for a whole family. For the alcohols it captures every member at once. If a chain has n carbons, an alcohol carries two-n-plus-one hydrogens plus the O-H group, so one formula stands for the whole family. <<WRITE_EQUATION:C_nH_{2n+1}OH|id=eq-1|boxed>> Here's an example from the chapter. Look at these four compounds: C H three O H, C two H five O H, C three H seven O H, and C four H nine O H. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Why are CH3OH, C2H5OH, C3H7OH and C4H9OH grouped together?|id=ex-q-1>> Notice what they all share. The only difference between them is <<FOCUS:methanol-chain+ethanol-chain+propanol-chain+butanol-chain>> the length of that chain. <<WRITE_STEP:All four contain the same functional group: alcohol (-OH)|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Because they carry the same functional group, their chemical properties are all very similar, regardless of how long the carbon chain grows. A series of compounds like this, where the same functional group substitutes for hydrogen along a carbon chain, is called a homologous series. <<WRITE_ANSWER:They form a homologous series — same functional group, very similar chemical properties.|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. Look at the formulae of successive compounds: methane is C H four, ethane is C two H six, propane is C three H eight, and butane is C four H ten. The question asks us to find the difference between successive members, and the difference in their molecular masses. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Methane CH4, ethane C2H6, propane C3H8, butane C4H10 — find the difference between successive members.|id=ex-q-1>> We start by comparing the first pair. Methane is C H four and ethane is C two H six. Ethane has one more carbon and two more hydrogens, so these differ by a C H two unit. <<WRITE_STEP:CH4 -> C2H6 : difference = CH2|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now compare ethane, C two H six, with propane, C three H eight. Again, one more carbon and two more hydrogens. And propane, C three H eight, compared with butane, C four H ten, gives the same result. So every successive pair differs by a C H two unit. <<WRITE_STEP:C2H6 -> C3H8 -> C4H10 : each pair differs by CH2|id=ex-step-1-2>> Next we find the difference in molecular masses. The atomic mass of carbon is twelve u and the atomic mass of hydrogen is one u. A C H two unit has one carbon and two hydrogens, so its mass is twelve plus two times one. <<WRITE_STEP:Mass of CH2 = (1 x 12) + (2 x 1)|id=ex-step-1-3>> That works out to twelve plus two, which equals fourteen u. So each successive member of the homologous series differs by a C H two unit, and that corresponds to a fixed mass difference of fourteen u. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Difference = CH2 unit = 12 + 2 = 14 u|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. Let's look at the homologous series for alkenes. The first member of this series is ethene. The members that follow have the formulas C three H six, C four H eight, and C five H ten. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Do the alkenes (ethene, C3H6, C4H8, C5H10) differ by a CH2 unit?|id=ex-q-1>> Let's check the difference between successive members. That word is not magic, it is a code. Here is the secret. Every carbon compound's name is built from <<FOCUS:stem-block+prefix-slot>> a piece you count and a piece you attach. <<UNFOCUS>> Let us decode it. <<SECTION:Counting the carbons|id=sec-1>> First, <<FOCUS:carbon-chain>> count the carbon atoms in the chain, because that number fixes the heart of the name. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> One carbon gives meth, two gives eth, three gives prop, four gives but. So this three-carbon chain <<FOCUS:stem-block>> hands us the stem prop. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:meth, eth, prop, but = 1,2,3,4 carbons|id=text-1>> Now, if the chain has only plain single bonds, <<FOCUS:ending-tag>> we tag on the ending ane. <<UNFOCUS>> Three carbons, all single bonds, becomes propane. But here is a question. What if our molecule is not just a plain chain, but carries something special, like the oxygen group that makes alcohol? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Naming the group|id=sec-2>> Then we announce that group in the name itself, using <<FOCUS:prefix-slot>> a phrase before, a prefix, or <<FOCUS:suffix-slot>> a phrase after, a suffix. A prefix like chloro <<FOCUS:prefix-slot>> sits at the front. A suffix like ol or one <<FOCUS:suffix-slot>> sits at the back. <<UNFOCUS>> Same stem, different attachment, different molecule. <<WRITE_KEY:Name = carbon-count stem + group prefix or suffix|id=key-1>> So the full rule is simply this: <<FOCUS:stem-block>> a stem that counts the carbons, <<FOCUS:prefix-slot+suffix-slot>> plus a prefix or suffix that names the group. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now one neat trick. When the suffix begins with a vowel, like the one in propanone, two vowels would collide awkwardly. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:propane minus e plus one = propanone|id=step-1>> So we <<FOCUS:stem-block>> drop the final e from the stem. <<UNFOCUS>> Propane loses its e, then we add one, giving propanone. Clean and smooth. Here's an example from the chapter. We have a three-carbon chain, and its functional group is a ketone. We need to name this compound. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Name a three-carbon chain with a ketone group|id=ex-q-1>> We start from the parent name for a three-carbon chain, which is propane. <<WRITE_STEP:Parent chain (three carbons) = propane|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now, the suffix for a ketone is one, and it begins with a vowel. So following our rule, we delete the final e from propane to get propan. <<WRITE_STEP:propane minus final e = propan|id=ex-step-1-2>> Then we add the suffix one to propan, which gives us propanone. <<WRITE_STEP:propan + one = propanone|id=ex-step-1-3>> And the answer is propanone. <<WRITE_ANSWER:propanone|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. When it's fully saturated, its base name is propane. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Name a three-carbon chain with a double bond, and with a triple bond.|id=ex-q-1>> The rule is simple: for an unsaturated chain, we replace the final 'ane' in propane. segments.narration_chapter: Every flame you have ever seen — a candle, a gas stove, a forest fire — is carbon coming apart and handing its energy to the world. Up to now you have learned how carbon atoms join into chains and rings. But building a molecule is only half the story — the exciting half is what these molecules DO when they react. <<SECTION:Chemical Properties of Carbon Compounds|id=sec-1>> And the single most important thing carbon compounds do is burn. We call this combustion, and it is the chemical property behind almost every fuel on Earth. <<PAUSE:short>> Here is what burning really is: a carbon compound grabs oxygen from the air, locks onto it tightly, and in doing so it spills out its stored energy as heat and light. <<WRITE_TEXT:Combustion = reacting with oxygen, releasing energy|id=text-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> When carbon meets enough oxygen, it joins with it completely to make carbon dioxide, and the leftover energy escapes as heat and light. <<WRITE_EQUATION:C + O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + \text{heat} + \text{light}|id=eq-1|boxed>> So when pure carbon meets plenty of oxygen, it combines completely to form carbon dioxide, and the energy left over rushes off as heat and light. But does it always burn this cleanly? What happens if there is not enough oxygen to go around? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Watch a fuel like methane: with enough oxygen it burns fully, giving carbon dioxide and water, and a clean burst of energy. <<WRITE_STEP:Fuel + plenty of oxygen gives carbon dioxide + water + energy|id=step-1>> A fuel like methane burns by combining with oxygen to give carbon dioxide and water, releasing a burst of energy. <<WRITE_EQUATION:CH_4 + 2O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + 2H_2O + \text{energy}|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:carbon_and_its_compounds:4_3:flame_comparison>> Now look at the board. On the left, a burner with plenty of air flowing in — see how <<FOCUS:blue-flame>> the flame is small, steady, and blue. <<FOCUS:oxygen-arrows-blue>> Those inward arrows are oxygen pouring in. <<UNFOCUS>> With this much oxygen, every carbon atom finds a partner and burns completely. <<FOCUS:blue-flame>> That clean blue flame is the signature of complete combustion. <<WRITE_KEY:Blue flame = complete combustion|id=key-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now starve the same flame of air. <<FOCUS:oxygen-arrows-yellow>> With only a few arrows of oxygen, the flame turns <<FOCUS:yellow-flame>> tall, yellow, and flickering. There is not enough oxygen for every carbon atom, so some carbon escapes unburnt — <<FOCUS:soot-particles>> these black specks are soot. <<FOCUS:yellow-flame>> A smoky yellow flame is the signature of incomplete combustion. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So next time you see a flame, read it like a chemist: combustion is carbon compounds meeting oxygen to release heat and light, and the colour tells you whether that meeting was complete or starved of air. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:carbon_and_its_compounds:4_3_1:flame_comparison>> Why does a candle flame <<FOCUS:yellow-flame>> glow yellow, but the flame on your kitchen stove burns a <<FOCUS:blue-flame>> clean, hissing blue? <<UNFOCUS>> The answer is hiding inside one word: burning. <<SECTION:Combustion|id=sec-1>> Burning has a proper name in chemistry: combustion. And here is the big idea — carbon, in every single form it comes in, burns in oxygen to give carbon dioxide, releasing heat and light. <<PAUSE:short>> Pure carbon plus oxygen gives carbon dioxide, and out comes heat and light. <<WRITE_EQUATION:C + O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + \text{heat} + \text{light}|id=eq-1|boxed>> It does not matter whether it is pure carbon, the methane in your stove, or the ethanol in a spirit lamp — the carbon always ends up locked into carbon dioxide, and any hydrogen ends up as water. Methane plus oxygen gives carbon dioxide and water, plus heat and light — the carbon becomes carbon dioxide and the hydrogen becomes water. <<WRITE_EQUATION:CH_4 + 2O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + 2H_2O + \text{heat} + \text{light}|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Combustion = combining with oxygen = oxidation|id=text-1>> This combining with oxygen is exactly what we call an oxidation reaction — combustion is just oxidation that happens fast enough to give off heat and light. <<PAUSE:short>> So back to our puzzle. If burning carbon always makes carbon dioxide, why does one flame come out clean and blue, and another come out yellow and smoky? <<PAUSE:long>> <<SECTION:Two kinds of flame|id=sec-2>> Look at <<FOCUS:blue-flame>> the blue flame. Its <<FOCUS:air-hole-open>> air hole is wide open, so <<FOCUS:air-in-left>> oxygen is pouring in. Every carbon atom finds enough oxygen to <<FOCUS:co2-products>> become carbon dioxide. <<UNFOCUS>> That is complete combustion. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Blue flame = complete combustion, plenty of oxygen|id=key-1>> A clean blue flame is the signature of complete combustion: lots of oxygen, all the carbon converted, and almost no smoke. <<PAUSE:short>> Now <<FOCUS:air-hole-closed>> close the air hole, and the story changes. <<UNFOCUS>> Starve the flame of oxygen, and the carbon cannot all reach carbon dioxide. The leftover unburnt carbon <<FOCUS:yellow-flame>> glows hot and yellow, then escapes as tiny black soot particles — watch them <<FOCUS:soot-deposit+soot-plate>> collect on a cold metal plate held over the flame. <<WRITE_KEY:Yellow sooty flame = incomplete combustion, too little oxygen|id=key-2>> So a <<FOCUS:yellow-flame>> yellow, sooty flame is the warning sign of incomplete combustion — the oxygen supply was simply too small. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Here's an example from the chapter on combustion. Carbon, in all its allotropic forms, burns in oxygen to release heat and light. The book gives us three reactions to look at: burning carbon itself, burning methane, and burning ethanol. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Write the combustion reactions for carbon, methane, and ethanol|id=ex-q-1>> Let's write them one by one. First, carbon plus oxygen gives carbon dioxide, plus heat and light. <<WRITE_STEP:C + O2 -> CO2 + heat and light|id=ex-step-1-1>> Next, methane plus oxygen gives carbon dioxide plus water, plus heat and light. <<WRITE_STEP:CH4 + 2 O2 -> CO2 + 2 H2O + heat and light|id=ex-step-1-2>> And ethanol plus oxygen gives carbon dioxide plus water, plus heat and light. <<WRITE_STEP:CH3CH2OH + 3 O2 -> 2 CO2 + 3 H2O + heat and light|id=ex-step-1-3>> Notice the pattern: in every case the fuel combines with oxygen, and oxygen is being added. So all of these are oxidation reactions, and each one releases heat and light. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Carbon, methane, and ethanol all burn in oxygen to give carbon dioxide (and water), releasing heat and light. These are oxidation reactions.|id=ex-ans-1>> There is a pattern here too: clean-burning saturated compounds tend to give a tidy flame, while unsaturated ones, packed with carbon, smoke more easily and leave that black deposit behind. So next time you see a flame, read its colour. <<FOCUS:blue-flame>> Blue means carbon fully fed with oxygen and turned cleanly into carbon dioxide; <<FOCUS:yellow-flame>> yellow and smoky means oxygen ran short. <<UNFOCUS>> The same combustion, just more or less air.

First, carbon plus oxygen gives carbon dioxide, plus heat and light. <<WRITE_STEP:C + O2 -> CO2 + heat and light|id=ex-step-1-1>> Next, methane plus oxygen gives carbon dioxide plus water, plus heat and light. <<WRITE_STEP:CH4 + 2 O2 -> CO2 + 2 H2O + heat and light|id=ex-step-1-2>> And ethanol plus oxygen gives carbon dioxide plus water, plus heat and light. <<WRITE_STEP:CH3CH2OH + 3 O2 -> 2 CO2 + 3 H2O + heat and light|id=ex-step-1-3>> Notice the pattern: in every case the fuel combines with oxygen, and oxygen is being added. These are oxidation reactions.|id=ex-ans-1>> There is a pattern here too: clean-burning saturated compounds tend to give a tidy flame, while unsaturated ones, packed with carbon, smoke more easily and leave that black deposit behind. <<POINT:soot-deposit>> <<FOCUS:blue-flame>> So next time you see a flame, read its colour. segments.narration_chapter: Here's a puzzle: how do you turn the alcohol in wine into the sour stuff in vinegar, without ever lighting a match? <<PAUSE:long>> You already know one violent way carbon compounds grab oxygen: combustion. Strike a match, and ethanol burns completely, releasing a burst of heat. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:carbon_and_its_compounds:4_3_2:oxidation_ladder>> <<SECTION:Gentle oxidation|id=sec-1>> But there's a gentler path. Instead of burning the alcohol away, we add just a little oxygen and stop. That controlled addition of oxygen is what we call oxidation. <<PAUSE:short>> Picture a ladder. On the <<FOCUS:ethanol-box+lower-rung>> lower rung sits ethanol, our alcohol. <<UNFOCUS>> We want to climb just one step up. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Oxidation = adding oxygen: alcohol to carboxylic acid|id=key-1>> <<FOCUS:oxidation-arrow+oxygen-tag>> Add oxygen, and the alcohol is <<FOCUS:acid-box+upper-rung>> transformed into a carboxylic acid sitting on the rung above. <<UNFOCUS>> That single step is oxidation. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:ethanol + oxygen to ethanoic acid|id=text-1>> So <<FOCUS:ethanol-box>> ethanol, the alcohol in wine, <<FOCUS:acid-box>> becomes ethanoic acid, the sour acid in vinegar. <<UNFOCUS>> No flame needed, just oxygen, added carefully. But oxygen doesn't just appear. Something has to hand it over. Who is the generous donor? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Oxidising agent donates the oxygen|id=key-2>> The donor is a substance <<FOCUS:agent-label>> called an oxidising agent. <<UNFOCUS>> Alkaline potassium permanganate is one such agent: it carries oxygen and pushes it onto the alcohol. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:carbon_and_its_compounds:4_3_2:permanganate_colour>> <<SECTION:The colour test|id=sec-2>> Now here's the beautiful part you can actually watch. Potassium permanganate is <<FOCUS:purple-colour>> deep purple. Drop it onto warm ethanol, and <<FOCUS:tube-initial+tube-initial-liquid>> the very first drops vanish, going colourless. <<UNFOCUS>> Why does the purple disappear at first? Because the permanganate is busy giving its oxygen to the alcohol, and in doing so it loses its colour. <<PAUSE:short>> Keep adding it, though, and suddenly <<FOCUS:tube-excess+purple-hatch>> the purple stays. <<UNFOCUS>> Why won't it fade any more? <<PAUSE:long>> Here's an example from the chapter. We take about three millilitres of ethanol in a test tube and warm it gently in a water bath. Then we add a five percent solution of alkaline potassium permanganate drop by drop. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Add alkaline KMnO4 drop by drop to warm ethanol. Why does the purple colour first disappear, then persist?|id=ex-q-1>> We start by watching the first few drops. <<FOCUS:drop+drop-arrow>> As each drop of the purple permanganate enters, <<FOCUS:tube-initial-liquid>> the colour disappears, because the permanganate is oxidising the ethanol, turning it into ethanoic acid. <<WRITE_STEP:Step 1: First drops added → purple colour disappears as ethanol is oxidised to ethanoic acid|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now we keep adding more, in excess. With nothing left to give its oxygen to, the excess permanganate keeps its purple. The persisting colour is the signal the reaction is finished. segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:carbon_and_its_compounds:4_3_3:addition_reaction_bond>> The same liquid vegetable oil in your kitchen can be turned into solid ghee — and the only thing that changes is one reaction that fills in its empty bonds. Look at this molecule. These two carbon atoms are <<FOCUS:double-bond>> joined by a double bond — two lines instead of one — which is the signature of an unsaturated hydrocarbon. Here is the key idea: that second line is like a stretched-out spare hand. <<UNFOCUS>> The carbons would actually rather hold something else with it, so the molecule is itching to react. So what happens if we bring in hydrogen? Will those carbons just sit there, or will they grab onto it? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Adding hydrogen|id=sec-1>> One of the two lines of the double bond breaks open, leaving a spare slot on each carbon — <<FOCUS:free-slot-left+free-slot-right>> one here, and one here. A hydrogen atom snaps into each open slot — <<FOCUS:hydrogen-left>> one onto the left carbon, <<FOCUS:hydrogen-right>> one onto the right carbon, added straight across the bond. <<PAUSE:short>> Now <<FOCUS:single-bond>> only a single bond is left between the carbons, every spare hand is full, and the molecule has <<FOCUS:product-label>> become saturated. <<UNFOCUS>> We added atoms without throwing anything away — that is why it is called an addition reaction. <<PAUSE:short>> Ethene, which has a double bond, plus hydrogen, <<FOCUS:catalyst-label>> in the presence of a nickel catalyst, gives ethane, which has only single bonds. <<WRITE_EQUATION:C_2H_4 + H_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Ni}} C_2H_6|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<UNFOCUS>> But there is a catch — left alone, hydrogen and the double bond mostly ignore each other. The reaction barely happens. So how do we actually make this reaction go? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Catalyst speeds up the reaction but is not used up|id=key-1>> We add a catalyst — <<FOCUS:catalyst-label>> a metal like nickel or palladium. <<UNFOCUS>> It helps the reaction along, and crucially, it comes out completely unchanged at the end, ready to do it again. <<PAUSE:short>> This exact reaction is hydrogenation. It is how runny vegetable oil, full of double bonds, is turned into a solid fat by filling those bonds with hydrogen over a nickel catalyst. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Addition: H adds across C=C double bond, unsaturated becomes saturated|id=key-2>> So remember the whole story: hydrogen adds across the double bond, the unsaturated molecule becomes saturated, and a catalyst makes it happen without being consumed. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:carbon_and_its_compounds:4_3_4:methane_substitution>> Methane is so unreactive you can mix it with chlorine in a dark bottle and almost nothing happens. Flip on a light, and within seconds the same mixture reacts. <<SECTION:Substitution Reaction|id=sec-1>> Light isn't a chemical you can pour in, so how on earth can switching it on cause a chemical reaction? <<PAUSE:long>> First, let's meet our lazy molecule. Methane is a saturated hydrocarbon, <<FOCUS:central-carbon>> a central carbon holding <<FOCUS:hydrogen-top+hydrogen-others>> four hydrogen atoms with single bonds only. <<WRITE_TEXT:Saturated = single bonds only, unreactive|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Because every bond is a single bond, there are no weak spots for a chemical to grab onto, so methane just sits there, inert in front of most reagents. <<PAUSE:short>> <<PAUSE:short>> Now here is the trigger. Sunlight carries energy, and that energy is enough to <<FOCUS:incoming-chlorine>> split a chlorine molecule into reactive pieces that go hunting for hydrogen. <<UNFOCUS>> Watch what the chlorine does. It pushes in and <<FOCUS:hydrogen-top>> takes the place of one hydrogen atom on the carbon, <<FOCUS:substituted-chlorine>> bonding to the carbon itself. And the hydrogen that got kicked out doesn't vanish, it pairs up with a chlorine and <<FOCUS:ejected-hcl>> leaves as hydrogen chloride gas. <<WRITE_KEY:Substitution: one atom takes the place of another|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> That swap is the whole idea. One atom takes the place of another, and we call it a substitution reaction. <<PAUSE:short>> Methane plus chlorine, in the presence of sunlight, gives chloromethane plus hydrogen chloride. <<WRITE_EQUATION:CH_4 + Cl_2 \xrightarrow{\text{sunlight}} CH_3Cl + HCl|id=eq-1|boxed>> In symbols, methane plus chlorine under sunlight gives chloromethane plus hydrogen chloride. The products are chloromethane and hydrogen chloride. <<WRITE_ANSWER:CH4 + Cl2 --(sunlight)--> CH3Cl + HCl|id=ex-ans-1>> And it doesn't have to stop at one. Chlorine can keep replacing the hydrogens one by one, so with bigger alkanes you usually get a whole family of products. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Sunlight triggers chlorine to substitute hydrogens|id=key-2>> So remember the two-part story: saturated hydrocarbons are unreactive, but sunlight triggers chlorine to substitute their hydrogen atoms, one at a time. <<PAUSE:short>>

What is it? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> It's ethanol, and the strange thing is you've already met it everywhere without knowing it was all the same molecule. <<SECTION:Ethanol|id=sec-1>> Remember the big idea about carbon: every carbon atom makes four bonds, and it can join to other carbons to build chains. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:carbon_and_its_compounds:4_4:ethanol_structure>> So let's build ethanol from scratch. Here is <<FOCUS:carbon-one>> one carbon atom, and we <<FOCUS:hydrogen-atoms>> hang three hydrogens off it. Two carbons, a handful of hydrogens, and one O-H group sitting on the end. Now here's the question worth pausing on: with all these atoms, which part actually makes ethanol behave the way it does? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:The O-H group is the business end of ethanol|id=key-1>> It's <<FOCUS:hydroxyl-highlight>> that O-H group. segments.narration_chapter: There's a single liquid that doctors put into your cough syrup to keep you well, and that in its pure form can kill you with a few sips. It's the same molecule. Meet ethanol. Most people just call it alcohol. At room temperature it sits there as a clear liquid, and it's the ingredient that makes alcoholic drinks alcoholic. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:carbon_and_its_compounds:4_4_1:ethanol_molecule>> <<SECTION:What makes ethanol special|id=sec-1>> So why is this little molecule everywhere in medicine? Let's actually look at it. Here are <<FOCUS:carbon-chain>> two carbon atoms with their hydrogens, a tiny chain. By itself that part is oily and doesn't care much for water. <<UNFOCUS>> But look at this end. There's an oxygen bonded to a hydrogen, <<FOCUS:oh-group>> the O-H group, and this little corner loves water. <<UNFOCUS>> So if I pour ethanol into water, what do you think happens at the boundary between them? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Ethanol mixes with water in ANY proportion|id=key-1>> There is no boundary. <<FOCUS:oh-group+water-side>> The O-H end grabs onto water and ethanol dissolves into it completely, in any proportion you like, a little or a lot. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> And it's not just water. Because ethanol has <<FOCUS:carbon-chain+oh-group>> both an oily side and a water-loving side, it dissolves a huge range of substances. <<UNFOCUS>> That makes it a brilliant solvent. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Good solvent: tincture iodine, cough syrups, tonics|id=text-1>> That's exactly why you find ethanol in tincture iodine, in cough syrups, and in many tonics, carrying medicine into a form you can swallow. But now the dark side. Drinking small amounts of dilute ethanol causes drunkenness, and even though it's a widespread habit, it harms the body and is best avoided. Here's an example from the chapter. We take a small piece of sodium metal, about the size of a couple of grains of rice, and drop it into ethanol, which is absolute alcohol. The question is: what happens, and what products form? <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Drop a small piece of sodium into ethanol (absolute alcohol). What reaction occurs?|id=ex-q-1>> As soon as the sodium touches the ethanol, a reaction begins. Alcohols react with sodium, and right away you see hydrogen gas evolved, bubbling off as the metal reacts. Let's write the balanced reaction: two sodium plus two ethanol gives two sodium ethoxide plus hydrogen gas. <<WRITE_STEP:two Na + two CH3CH2OH → two CH3CH2O−Na+ + H2|id=ex-step-1-1>> So the answer is clear. Hydrogen gas is evolved during the reaction, and the other product is sodium ethoxide. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Hydrogen gas is evolved; the other product is sodium ethoxide.|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. We heat ethanol at four hundred forty-three kelvin using excess concentrated sulphuric acid, and we want to find out what we get. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Heat ethanol at 443 K with excess conc. sulphuric acid — what forms?|id=ex-q-1>> Here the concentrated sulphuric acid acts as a dehydrating agent, which means it removes water from the ethanol. Stripping out that water from ethanol leaves behind the unsaturated hydrocarbon ethene. <<WRITE_STEP:Conc. H2SO4 = dehydrating agent, removes water from ethanol|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:CH_3CH_2OH \xrightarrow{\text{Hot Conc. } H_2SO_4} CH_2{=}CH_2 + H_2O|id=ex-eq-1>> And the answer is that the products are ethene and water. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Products: ethene (CH2=CH2) and water|id=ex-ans-1>> <<WRITE_KEY:Pure ethanol (absolute alcohol) can be lethal|id=key-2>> And pure ethanol, what chemists call absolute alcohol, is lethal even in a small quantity. The very same molecule that heals can kill. <<PAUSE:short>> So remember the two faces of ethanol: a liquid that mixes with water in any proportion and dissolves countless substances, yet one that is genuinely dangerous when pure or consumed. Useful and harmful, all in one tiny molecule. <<PAUSE:short>>

At room temperature it sits there as a clear liquid, and it's the ingredient that makes alcoholic drinks alcoholic. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:carbon-chain>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:carbon_and_its_compounds:4_4_1:ethanol_molecule>> <<SECTION:What makes ethanol special|id=sec-1>>So why is this little molecule everywhere in medicine? Let's actually look at it. Here are two carbon atoms with their hydrogens, a tiny chain. By itself that part is oily and doesn't care much for water. <<POINT:carbon-chain>> <<FOCUS:oh-group>> But look at this end. There's an oxygen bonded to a hydrogen, the O-H group, and this little corner loves water. So if I pour ethanol into water, what do you think happens at the boundary between them? <<POINT:water-side>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:water-side>> <<WRITE_KEY:Ethanol mixes with water in ANY proportion|id=key-1>>There is no boundary. The O-H end grabs onto water and ethanol dissolves into it completely, in any proportion you like, a little or a lot. <<TRACE:water-side>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:oh-group>> And it's not just water. Because ethanol has both an oily side and a water-loving side, it dissolves a huge range of substances. That makes it a brilliant solvent. <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Good solvent: tincture iodine, cough syrups, tonics|id=text-1>>That's exactly why you find ethanol in tincture iodine, in cough syrups, and in many tonics, carrying medicine into a form you can swallow. But now the dark side. Drinking small amounts of dilute ethanol causes drunkenness, and even though it's a widespread habit, it harms the body and is best avoided. Here's an example from the chapter. We take a small piece of sodium metal, about the size of a couple of grains of rice, and drop it into ethanol, which is absolute alcohol. The question is: what happens, and what products form? <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Drop a small piece of sodium into ethanol (absolute alcohol). What reaction occurs?|id=ex-q-1>> As soon as the sodium touches the ethanol, a reaction begins. Alcohols react with sodium, and right away you see hydrogen gas evolved, bubbling off as the metal reacts. Let's write the balanced reaction: two sodium plus two ethanol gives two sodium ethoxide plus hydrogen gas. <<WRITE_STEP:two Na + two CH3CH2OH → two CH3CH2O−Na+ + H2|id=ex-step-1-1>> So the answer is clear. Hydrogen gas is evolved during the reaction, and the other product is sodium ethoxide. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Hydrogen gas is evolved; the other product is sodium ethoxide.|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. We heat ethanol at four hundred forty-three kelvin using excess concentrated sulphuric acid, and we want to find out what we get. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Heat ethanol at 443 K with excess conc. sulphuric acid — what forms?|id=ex-q-1>> Here the concentrated sulphuric acid acts as a dehydrating agent, which means it removes water from the ethanol. Stripping out that water from ethanol leaves behind the unsaturated hydrocarbon ethene. <<WRITE_STEP:Conc. H2SO4 = dehydrating agent, removes water from ethanol|id=ex-step-1-1>><<WRITE_EQUATION:CH_3CH_2OH \xrightarrow{\text{Hot Conc. } H_2SO_4} CH_2{=}CH_2 + H_2O|id=ex-eq-1>> And the answer is that the products are ethene and water. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Products: ethene (CH2=CH2) and water|id=ex-ans-1>> <<WRITE_KEY:Pure ethanol (absolute alcohol) can be lethal|id=key-2>>And pure ethanol, what chemists call absolute alcohol, is lethal even in a small quantity. The very same molecule that heals can kill. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:oh-group>> So remember the two faces of ethanol: a liquid that mixes with water in any proportion and dissolves countless substances, yet one that is genuinely dangerous when pure or consumed. Useful and harmful, all in one tiny molecule. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: The sour kick in the vinegar on your chips is a real acid, and on a freezing winter morning that same pure acid can turn into ice-like crystals that look just like a glacier. That acid is ethanoic acid, which most people call acetic acid, and it belongs to a family called the carboxylic acids. <<SECTION:Meet Ethanoic Acid|id=sec-1>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Ethanoic acid = acetic acid, a carboxylic acid|id=text-1>> Pure ethanoic acid freezes at two hundred ninety kelvin, just below room temperature, so in cold climates it solidifies into glassy crystals, earning the nickname glacial acetic acid. Dilute it in water to about five to eight percent and you get vinegar, the sour liquid that preserves pickles in your kitchen. Now here is the real question: vinegar is an acid, but is it as strong an acid as something like hydrochloric acid? <<PAUSE:long>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:carbon_and_its_compounds:4_4_2:ionisation_comparison>> To answer that, let's look at what actually happens <<FOCUS:hcl-beaker+ethanoic-beaker>> when each acid dissolves in water. <<SECTION:Strong versus weak|id=sec-2>> In hydrochloric acid, almost every single molecule <<FOCUS:hcl-ions>> splits apart into a hydrogen ion and a chloride ion, flooding the water with hydrogen ions. But in ethanoic acid, <<FOCUS:ethanoic-molecules>> most of the molecules stay whole, and only a small fraction break apart to release hydrogen ions. <<PAUSE:short>> So here is the payoff: vinegar feels milder because <<FOCUS:few-h-ions>> only a few of its molecules ionise, while hydrochloric acid ionises almost completely. That is exactly what we mean by a <<FOCUS:ethanoic-beaker+hcl-beaker>> weak acid versus a strong acid. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Ethanoic acid only partly splits, so we write its ionisation with a two-way arrow showing most molecules stay whole. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{COO}^- + \text{H}^+|id=eq-1|boxed>> Press that home: ethanoic acid is a weak acid because only a few of its molecules ionise in water, whereas hydrochloric acid ionises almost completely. <<WRITE_KEY:Ethanoic acid = weak acid: only partially ionised in water|id=key-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> This is why if you test both with universal indicator, the same concentration of ethanoic acid shows a higher pH, a less intense colour, than hydrochloric acid. Being an acid, ethanoic acid does react, and one of its most charming reactions is with an alcohol. <<SECTION:Esterification|id=sec-3>> Here's an example from the chapter about ethanoic acid in everyday life. The vinegar you find in your kitchen is simply a five to eight percent solution of acetic acid in water, and it's used widely as a preservative in pickles. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Why is pure ethanoic acid called glacial acetic acid?|id=ex-q-1>> Ethanoic acid combines with ethanol, using an acid catalyst, to give an ester plus water. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} \xrightarrow{\text{acid}} \text{CH}_3\text{COOC}_2\text{H}_5 + \text{H}_2\text{O}|id=eq-2|boxed>> Now let's look at the pure form. The melting point of pure ethanoic acid is two hundred and ninety kelvin, which is just below ordinary room temperature. <<WRITE_STEP:Vinegar = 5 to 8 percent acetic acid in water (preservative)|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:Melting point of pure ethanoic acid = 290 kelvin|id=ex-step-1-2>> Because two hundred and ninety kelvin is so close to room temperature, pure ethanoic acid often freezes during winter in cold climates, forming ice-like crystals. That frozen, glacier-like appearance is exactly why pure ethanoic acid earned the name glacial acetic acid. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Pure ethanoic acid freezes near 290 K in cold winters, looking like glacier ice, hence the name glacial acetic acid.|id=ex-ans-1>> When ethanoic acid is warmed with an alcohol and a few drops of acid catalyst, they join together and release water, forming a compound called an ester. <<WRITE_TEXT:acid + alcohol -> ester + water|id=text-2>> <<PAUSE:short>> And the delightful part: that ester smells sweet and fruity, the same kind of scent used in perfumes and flavourings, so ethanoic acid plus an alcohol with an acid catalyst gives you a sweet-smelling ester through esterification. <<WRITE_KEY:Esterification: acid + alcohol --(acid catalyst)--> sweet-smelling ester|id=key-2>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: You can scrub a greasy plate with plain water all day and it stays greasy — so what does a tiny drop of soap do that water alone simply can't? <<PAUSE:long>> Here's the root of the problem: most dirt that clings to our clothes and skin is oily, and oil and water flatly refuse to mix. Shake them together however hard you like, and the oil just regroups and floats away. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:carbon_and_its_compounds:4_5:soap_molecule>> <<SECTION:The two-faced molecule|id=sec-1>> So plain water is helpless against grease. Soap solves this with a molecule that is, quite <<FOCUS:ionic-head+carbon-tail>> literally, two-faced. One end is a <<FOCUS:carbon-tail>> long chain of carbon atoms. This tail hates water but loves oil — it will happily bury itself in grease. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Head = ionic, water-loving; tail = carbon chain, oil-loving|id=text-1>> The other end is <<FOCUS:ionic-head>> an ionic head — it carries a charge, and it loves water. So one molecule <<FOCUS:carbon-tail>> reaches out to grease with its tail while <<FOCUS:ionic-head>> clinging to water with its head. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now here's the puzzle: a single molecule has just one tail. How can these tiny things gang up to pull a whole droplet of grease off your plate and into the water? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:carbon_and_its_compounds:4_5:micelle>> <<SECTION:The micelle|id=sec-2>> Watch what happens when <<FOCUS:oil-droplet>> many soap molecules meet one oil droplet. <<FOCUS:micelle-tails>> Every tail dives into the oil, and <<FOCUS:micelle-heads>> every head turns to face the water outside. <<UNFOCUS>> The tails crowd inward, hidden inside the grease where they're happy. <<WRITE_KEY:Soap surrounds oil: tails in, heads out = a micelle|id=key-1>> And <<FOCUS:micelle-heads+water-surround>> all the ionic heads point outward into the water, forming a tidy ball with the grease trapped at its centre. This structure is <<FOCUS:micelle-label>> called a micelle. <<PAUSE:short>> Because its outside is now all water-loving heads, the whole greasy ball is <<FOCUS:water-surround>> welcomed by the water — and the droplet that water alone could never touch gets lifted away and rinsed down the drain. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So remember this: soap works because one molecule has two ends with opposite tastes — a water-loving head and an oil-loving tail. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Detergents work the same way; clean even in hard water|id=text-2>> Detergents clean by exactly the same trick, with a head built to keep working even in hard water — but the heart of it is always that two-faced molecule wrapping grease into a micelle. <<PAUSE:short>>
