Acetic acid melts at two hundred ninety kelvin and boils at three hundred ninety-one kelvin. <<WRITE_STEP:Acetic acid: melts 290 K, boils 391 K|id=ex-step-1-1>> Chloroform melts at two hundred nine kelvin and boils at three hundred thirty-four kelvin. <<WRITE_STEP:Chloroform: melts 209 K, boils 334 K|id=ex-step-1-2>> Ethanol melts at one hundred fifty-six kelvin and boils at three hundred fifty-one kelvin. <<WRITE_STEP:Ethanol: melts 156 K, boils 351 K|id=ex-step-1-3>> And methane melts at just ninety kelvin and boils at one hundred eleven kelvin. <<WRITE_STEP:Methane: melts 90 K, boils 111 K|id=ex-step-1-4>>

segments.raw_narration: Here's an example from the chapter. Carbon has an atomic number of six, which means it has four electrons in its outermost shell. To reach a stable noble gas configuration, it needs to either gain or lose four electrons. Let's see why neither of those options works well. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Why can't carbon simply gain or lose four electrons?|id=ex-q-1>>
segments.text_with_markers: Here's an example from the chapter. Carbon has an atomic number of six, which means it has four electrons in its outermost shell. To reach a stable noble gas configuration, it needs to either gain or lose four electrons. Let's see why neither of those options works well. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Why can't carbon simply gain or lose four electrons?|id=ex-q-1>>

segments.raw_narration: First, consider gaining. If carbon gains four electrons, it forms a C four minus anion. But now its nucleus, which has only six protons, would have to hold on to ten electrons, that is, four extra electrons. That's a real struggle for such a small nucleus. <<WRITE_STEP:Option 1 — Gain 4 electrons: forms C4- with 10 electrons, but 6 protons can't hold 10 electrons|id=ex-step-1-1>>
segments.text_with_markers: First, consider gaining. If carbon gains four electrons, it forms a C four minus anion. But now its nucleus, which has only six protons, would have to hold on to ten electrons, that is, four extra electrons. That's a real struggle for such a small nucleus. <<WRITE_STEP:Option 1 — Gain 4 electrons: forms C4- with 10 electrons, but 6 protons can't hold 10 electrons|id=ex-step-1-1>>

segments.raw_narration: Now consider losing. If carbon loses four electrons, it forms a C four plus cation, leaving the six protons in its nucleus holding on to just two electrons. But pulling four electrons away requires a huge amount of energy. So neither route is favorable, and that is exactly why carbon chooses to share electrons instead. <<WRITE_STEP:Option 2 — Lose 4 electrons: forms C4+ with 2 electrons, but removing 4 electrons needs too much energy|id=ex-step-1-2>>
segments.text_with_markers: Now consider losing. If carbon loses four electrons, it forms a C four plus cation, leaving the six protons in its nucleus holding on to just two electrons. But pulling four electrons away requires a huge amount of energy. So neither route is favorable, and that is exactly why carbon chooses to share electrons instead. <<WRITE_STEP:Option 2 — Lose 4 electrons: forms C4+ with 2 electrons, but removing 4 electrons needs too much energy|id=ex-step-1-2>>

segments.raw_narration: And the conclusion is this: because carbon cannot easily gain or lose four electrons, it attains a stable configuration by sharing electrons instead. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Carbon shares electrons rather than gaining or losing four|id=ex-ans-1>>
segments.text_with_markers: And the conclusion is this: because carbon cannot easily gain or lose four electrons, it attains a stable configuration by sharing electrons instead. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Carbon shares electrons rather than gaining or losing four|id=ex-ans-1>>

segments.raw_narration: Here's an example from the chapter, the simplest covalent molecule of all. The atomic number of hydrogen is one, so hydrogen has just one electron in its K shell, and it needs one more electron to fill that K shell. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: How do two hydrogen atoms bond to form H2?|id=ex-q-1>>
segments.text_with_markers: Here's an example from the chapter, the simplest covalent molecule of all. The atomic number of hydrogen is one, so hydrogen has just one electron in its K shell, and it needs one more electron to fill that K shell. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: How do two hydrogen atoms bond to form H2?|id=ex-q-1>>

segments.raw_narration: So here's what the two atoms do. Two hydrogen atoms share their electrons, contributing one electron each, to form a molecule of hydrogen, H two. <<WRITE_STEP:Hydrogen, atomic number 1, has 1 electron in K shell and needs 1 more.|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:Two H atoms each share one electron to form H2.|id=ex-step-1-2>>

Two hydrogen atoms share their electrons, contributing one electron each, to form a molecule of hydrogen, H two. <<WRITE_STEP:Hydrogen, atomic number 1, has 1 electron in K shell and needs 1 more.|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:Two H atoms each share one electron to form H2.|id=ex-step-1-2>>

segments.raw_narration: By sharing, each hydrogen atom now attains the configuration of the nearest noble gas, helium, which has two electrons in its K shell. And that one shared pair of electrons constitutes a single covalent bond between the two hydrogen atoms. <<WRITE_ANSWER:H2 forms by one shared pair = one single covalent bond; each H attains helium's stable 2-electron K shell.|id=ex-ans-1>>

segments.raw_narration: Here's an example from the chapter, on how oxygen molecules form. An atom of oxygen has an atomic number of eight, which means it carries six electrons in its outer L shell. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: How do two oxygen atoms bond to complete their octets?|id=ex-q-1>>
segments.text_with_markers: Here's an example from the chapter, on how oxygen molecules form. An atom of oxygen has an atomic number of eight, which means it carries six electrons in its outer L shell. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: How do two oxygen atoms bond to complete their octets?|id=ex-q-1>>

segments.raw_narration: We start by asking what oxygen needs. With six electrons in its L shell, each oxygen atom needs two more electrons to complete its octet. So each atom of oxygen shares two electrons with another oxygen atom. <<WRITE_STEP:Each oxygen has 6 electrons in L shell, needs 2 more|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:Each oxygen shares 2 electrons with the other|id=ex-step-1-2>>

So each atom of oxygen shares two electrons with another oxygen atom. <<WRITE_STEP:Each oxygen has 6 electrons in L shell, needs 2 more|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:Each oxygen shares 2 electrons with the other|id=ex-step-1-2>>

segments.raw_narration: The two electrons contributed by each oxygen atom give rise to two shared pairs of electrons, and two shared pairs equal a double bond. So the answer is, a double bond forms between the two oxygen atoms. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Two shared pairs = a double bond between the two oxygen atoms|id=ex-ans-1>>

segments.text_with_markers: Here's an example from the chapter. What would happen in the case of a diatomic molecule of nitrogen? Nitrogen has the atomic number seven. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: How does a diatomic nitrogen molecule bond?|id=ex-q-1>>

segments.raw_narration: With atomic number seven, each nitrogen atom needs to attain an octet. To do this, each nitrogen atom contributes three electrons. <<WRITE_STEP:Each nitrogen contributes three electrons to attain an octet|id=ex-step-1-1>>

segments.raw_narration: Those contributed electrons give rise to three shared pairs of electrons, and three shared pairs constitute a triple bond between the two atoms. So the answer is that nitrogen forms a triple bond. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Three shared pairs of electrons form a triple bond between the two nitrogen atoms|id=ex-ans-1>>

segments.text_with_markers: Here's an example from the chapter. Let us take a look at methane, which is a compound of carbon. Methane has the formula C H four. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: How does carbon bond with hydrogen to form methane (CH4)?|id=ex-q-1>>

segments.raw_narration: We start with what we know about the atoms. Hydrogen, as you know, has a valency of one. Carbon is tetravalent because it has four valence electrons. <<WRITE_STEP:Hydrogen valency = 1; Carbon has 4 valence electrons (tetravalent)|id=ex-step-1-1>>

segments.raw_narration: In order to achieve a noble gas configuration, carbon shares these electrons with four atoms of hydrogen. Each shared pair forms one covalent bond. <<WRITE_STEP:Carbon shares its 4 electrons, one with each of 4 hydrogen atoms|id=ex-step-1-2>>

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Why carbon?|id=sec-1>>That is a staggering imbalance, so there must be something special about this one little atom. It comes down to the way carbon shares electrons to make covalent bonds.
segments.text_with_markers: <<SECTION:Why carbon?|id=sec-1>>That is a staggering imbalance, so there must be something special about this one little atom. It comes down to the way carbon shares electrons to make covalent bonds.

segments.raw_narration: Here is the trick. A carbon atom can bond not just to other elements, but to other carbon atoms — over and over again.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:straight-chain>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:carbon_and_its_compounds:4_2:carbon_skeletons>> Here is the trick. A carbon atom can bond not just to other elements, but to other carbon atoms — over and over again. <<TRACE:straight-chain>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: Picture carbon atoms linking hands. They can form a long straight chain like this, one carbon holding the next, holding the next.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:straight-chain>> Picture carbon atoms linking hands. They can form a long straight chain like this, one carbon holding the next, holding the next.

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_KEY:Catenation = carbon bonding to carbon, in chains, branches and rings|id=key-1>>But they need not stay in a straight line. A chain can branch off in a new direction, or even curl around and join up into a ring. This linking-up is called catenation.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:branched-chain>> <<WRITE_KEY:Catenation = carbon bonding to carbon, in chains, branches and rings|id=key-1>>But they need not stay in a straight line. A chain can branch off in a new direction, or even curl around and join up into a ring. This linking-up is called catenation. <<TRACE:branched-chain>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: And the links themselves can vary — carbon atoms can be joined by single bonds, or by double bonds, or even triple bonds.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:double-bond-link>> And the links themselves can vary — carbon atoms can be joined by single bonds, or by double bonds, or even triple bonds. <<POINT:double-bond-link>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_TEXT:chains + branches + rings + bond types = millions|id=text-1>>Now think about how many different molecules you can build by mixing chains, branches, rings, and three kinds of bond. That combination explosion is exactly where the millions come from.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:carbon-ring>> <<WRITE_TEXT:chains + branches + rings + bond types = millions|id=text-1>>Now think about how many different molecules you can build by mixing chains, branches, rings, and three kinds of bond. That combination explosion is exactly where the millions come from. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: But here is the puzzle — silicon sits right below carbon and also makes four bonds. So why does silicon only manage chains of seven or eight atoms, while carbon goes on almost forever?
segments.text_with_markers: <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> But here is the puzzle — silicon sits right below carbon and also makes four bonds. So why does silicon only manage chains of seven or eight atoms, while carbon goes on almost forever? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Why carbon and not silicon?|id=sec-2>>The answer is size. Carbon is a tiny atom, so its shared electrons sit very close to both nuclei.

segments.raw_narration: With four bonding arms and that small size, the bond between two carbon atoms is held together extremely tightly — it is strong and stable.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:four-arms>> With four bonding arms and that small size, the bond between two carbon atoms is held together extremely tightly — it is strong and stable. <<POINT:four-arms>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: Silicon is a bigger atom. Its shared electrons are further from the nuclei, so silicon-to-silicon bonds are weaker and the chains fall apart quickly.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:silicon-comparison>> Silicon is a bigger atom. Its shared electrons are further from the nuclei, so silicon-to-silicon bonds are weaker and the chains fall apart quickly. <<POINT:silicon-comparison>>

segments.raw_narration: So remember this — catenation, carbon's gift for bonding endlessly to itself in chains, branches and rings, is the single biggest reason there are millions of carbon compounds, and its small strong bonds are why carbon, and no other element, pulls it off.

segments.raw_narration: What if you could pluck one hydrogen off a carbon chain, snap something else into its place, and completely change what the molecule does?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:carbon-chain>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:carbon_and_its_compounds:4_2_3:chain_swap>> What if you could pluck one hydrogen off a carbon chain, snap something else into its place, and completely change what the molecule does?

segments.raw_narration: So far carbon has only made friends with hydrogen, giving us those chains and rings we call hydrocarbons. <<SECTION:Carbon makes other friends|id=sec-1>>But carbon is a very friendly element, and hydrogen is not its only companion.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:hydrogen-atoms>> So far carbon has only made friends with hydrogen, giving us those chains and rings we call hydrocarbons. <<SECTION:Carbon makes other friends|id=sec-1>>But carbon is a very friendly element, and hydrogen is not its only companion.

segments.raw_narration: Carbon also happily bonds with the halogens, which are chlorine, bromine, fluorine, and iodine, and with oxygen, nitrogen, and sulphur. <<WRITE_TEXT:Carbon bonds: halogens, O, N, S too|id=text-1>>
segments.text_with_markers: Carbon also happily bonds with the halogens, which are chlorine, bromine, fluorine, and iodine, and with oxygen, nitrogen, and sulphur. <<WRITE_TEXT:Carbon bonds: halogens, O, N, S too|id=text-1>> <<POINT:hydrogen-atoms>>

segments.raw_narration: Here is the trick. Take one hydrogen hanging off the chain, and decide that this is the one we want to swap out.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:target-hydrogen>> Here is the trick. Take one hydrogen hanging off the chain, and decide that this is the one we want to swap out.

segments.raw_narration: Now, if we just yank that hydrogen off, won't carbon be left with a lonely, unsatisfied bond?
segments.text_with_markers: Now, if we just yank that hydrogen off, won't carbon be left with a lonely, unsatisfied bond? <<TRACE:free-valency>> <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: Yes, and that dangling bond is exactly the opening we need. We call it a free valency, and we fill it by snapping a new partner into place so carbon's bonding capacity of four stays perfectly satisfied.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:functional-group>> Yes, and that dangling bond is exactly the opening we need. We call it a free valency, and we fill it by snapping a new partner into place so carbon's bonding capacity of four stays perfectly satisfied.

segments.raw_narration: The element or group that replaces the hydrogen has a special name. <<WRITE_TEXT:Heteroatom = the atom replacing H|id=text-2>>A single replacing atom, like a chlorine or an oxygen, is called a heteroatom.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:functional-group>> The element or group that replaces the hydrogen has a special name. <<WRITE_TEXT:Heteroatom = the atom replacing H|id=text-2>>A single replacing atom, like a chlorine or an oxygen, is called a heteroatom.

segments.raw_narration: When that heteroatom comes as part of a recognisable group, attached through that single free valency, we call the whole thing a functional group.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:functional-group>> When that heteroatom comes as part of a recognisable group, attached through that single free valency, we call the whole thing a functional group. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: So replacing a hydrogen on a carbon chain with a heteroatom or group is what gives you a functional group. <<WRITE_KEY:Swap an H for a group = a functional group|id=key-1>>
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:functional-group>> So replacing a hydrogen on a carbon chain with a heteroatom or group is what gives you a functional group. <<WRITE_KEY:Swap an H for a group = a functional group|id=key-1>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: And here is the beautiful part. The functional group decides how the molecule behaves, regardless of whether the carbon chain is short or long, straight or branched.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:functional-group>> And here is the beautiful part. The functional group decides how the molecule behaves, regardless of whether the carbon chain is short or long, straight or branched. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: Whether you hang an O-H group on a two-carbon chain or a twenty-carbon chain, that O-H is what makes both behave like alcohols. <<WRITE_TEXT:Group sets properties, not chain length|id=text-3>>
segments.text_with_markers: Whether you hang an O-H group on a two-carbon chain or a twenty-carbon chain, that O-H is what makes both behave like alcohols. <<WRITE_TEXT:Group sets properties, not chain length|id=text-3>> <<POINT:carbon-chain>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: So carbon's friendliness is the whole story here: one swapped hydrogen, one new group, and an entirely new family of compounds with its own personality.

segments.raw_narration: Methanol, ethanol, propanol, butanol — four different chemicals, four different carbon chains, yet they all behave like cousins from the same family. Why?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:methanol-chain>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:carbon_and_its_compounds:4_2_4:alcohol_family_ladder>> Methanol, ethanol, propanol, butanol — four different chemicals, four different carbon chains, yet they all behave like cousins from the same family. Why? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: Here's the secret. Every one of these has the same little attachment on the end — the alcohol group, that oxygen-hydrogen pair.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:oh-group-column>> Here's the secret. Every one of these has the same little attachment on the end — the alcohol group, that oxygen-hydrogen pair.

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:The functional group rules|id=sec-1>>And that attachment is the boss. The functional group, not how long the carbon chain is, decides how the compound reacts.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:The functional group rules|id=sec-1>>And that attachment is the boss. The functional group, not how long the carbon chain is, decides how the compound reacts. <<POINT:oh-group-column>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: So whether the chain behind it is one carbon long or four carbons long, the chemistry stays basically the same. <<WRITE_KEY:Functional group decides the chemistry, not chain length|id=key-1>>
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:butanol-chain>> So whether the chain behind it is one carbon long or four carbons long, the chemistry stays basically the same. <<WRITE_KEY:Functional group decides the chemistry, not chain length|id=key-1>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: A family like this — same functional group sitting on carbon chains of growing length — has a name: a homologous series. <<WRITE_TEXT:Homologous series = same group, growing chain|id=text-1>>
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:oh-group-column>> A family like this — same functional group sitting on carbon chains of growing length — has a name: a homologous series. <<WRITE_TEXT:Homologous series = same group, growing chain|id=text-1>>

segments.raw_narration: Now look at how we climb from one rung to the next. Going from methanol up to ethanol, what exactly did we add?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:ethanol-chain>> Now look at how we climb from one rung to the next. Going from methanol up to ethanol, what exactly did we add? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: Just one extra carbon and two extra hydrogens — a single CH2 unit. And from ethanol to propanol, again one CH2. <<WRITE_TEXT:Each step adds one CH2|id=text-2>>
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:ch2-step>> Just one extra carbon and two extra hydrogens — a single CH2 unit. And from ethanol to propanol, again one CH2. <<WRITE_TEXT:Each step adds one CH2|id=text-2>>

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:The CH2 staircase|id=sec-2>>So every member of a homologous series differs from the next by exactly one CH2 unit. It's a perfectly regular staircase. <<WRITE_KEY:Successive members differ by one CH2|id=key-2>>
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:ch2-step>> <<SECTION:The CH2 staircase|id=sec-2>>So every member of a homologous series differs from the next by exactly one CH2 unit. It's a perfectly regular staircase. <<WRITE_KEY:Successive members differ by one CH2|id=key-2>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: Because each step adds the same CH2 unit, the molecular mass jumps by the same amount every time — that's a carbon at twelve plus two hydrogens, fourteen units heavier per step.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:propanol-chain>> Because each step adds the same CH2 unit, the molecular mass jumps by the same amount every time — that's a carbon at twelve plus two hydrogens, fourteen units heavier per step.

segments.raw_narration: This regularity is exactly why we can write one general formula for a whole family. For the alcohols it captures every member at once.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:butanol-chain>> This regularity is exactly why we can write one general formula for a whole family. For the alcohols it captures every member at once.

segments.raw_narration: If a chain has n carbons, an alcohol carries two-n-plus-one hydrogens plus the O-H group, so one formula stands for the whole family.

segments.raw_narration: Here's the root of the problem: most dirt that clings to our clothes and skin is oily, and oil and water flatly refuse to mix. Shake them together however hard you like, and the oil just regroups and floats away.

segments.raw_narration: One end is a long chain of carbon atoms. This tail hates water but loves oil — it will happily bury itself in grease.

4.1 BONDING IN CARBON – THE COVALENT BOND
In the previous Chapter, we have studied the properties of ionic
compounds. We saw that ionic compounds have high melting and boiling
points and conduct electricity in solution or in the molten state. We also

saw how the nature of bonding in ionic compounds explains these
properties. Let us now study the properties of some carbon compounds.
Most carbon compounds are poor conductors of electricity as we
have seen in Chapter 2. From the data
given in Table 4.1 on the boiling and
melting points of the carbon compounds,
we find that these compounds have low
melting and boiling points as compared
to ionic compounds (Chapter 3). We can
conclude that the forces of attraction
between the molecules are not very
strong. Since these compounds are
largely non-conductors of electricity, we
can conclude that the bonding in these
compounds does not give rise to any ions.
In Class IX, we learnt about the
combining capacity of various elements and how it depends on the
number of valence electrons. Let us now look at the electronic
configuration of carbon. The atomic number of carbon is 6. What would
be the distribution of electrons in various shells of carbon? How many
valence electrons will carbon have?
We know that the reactivity of elements is explained as their tendency
to attain a completely filled outer shell, that is, attain noble gas
configuration. Elements forming ionic compounds achieve this by either
gaining or losing electrons from the outermost shell. In the case of carbon,
it has four electrons in its outermost shell and needs to gain or lose four
electrons to attain noble gas configuration. If it were to gain or lose
electrons –
(i)
It could gain four electrons forming C4– anion. But it would be difficult
for the nucleus with six protons to hold on to ten electrons, that is,
four extra electrons.
(ii)
It could lose four electrons forming C4+ cation. But it would require
a large amount of energy to remove four electrons leaving behind a
carbon cation with six protons in its nucleus holding on to just two
electrons.
Carbon overcomes this problem by sharing its valence electrons with
other atoms of carbon or with atoms of other elements. Not just carbon,
but many other elements form molecules by sharing electrons in this
manner. The shared electrons ‘belong’ to the outermost shells of both
the atoms and lead to both atoms attaining the noble gas configuration.
Before going on to compounds of carbon, let us look at some simple
molecules formed by the sharing of valence electrons.
The simplest molecule formed in this manner is that of hydrogen.
As you have learnt earlier, the atomic number of hydrogen is 1. Hence
hydrogen has one electron in its K shell and it requires one more electron
to fill the K shell. So two hydrogen atoms share their electrons to form a
molecule of hydrogen, H2. This allows each hydrogen atom to attain the

The shared pair of electrons is said to constitute a
single covalent bond between the two hydrogen atoms.
A single covalent bond is also represented by a line
between the two atoms, as shown in Fig. 4.2.
The atomic number of chlorine is 17. What would be its electronic
configuration and its valency? Chlorine forms a diatomic molecule, Cl2.
Can you draw the electron dot structure for this molecule? Note that
only the valence shell electrons need to be depicted.
In the case of oxygen, we see the formation of a double bond between
two oxygen atoms. This is because an atom of oxygen has six electrons
in its L shell (the atomic number of oxygen is eight) and it requires two
more electrons to complete its octet. So each atom of oxygen shares two
electrons with another atom of oxygen to give us the structure shown in
Fig. 4.3. The two electrons contributed by each oxygen atom give rise to
two shared pairs of electrons. This is said to constitute a double bond
between the two atoms.
Can you now depict a molecule of water showing the nature
of bonding between one oxygen atom and two hydrogen
atoms? Does the molecule have single bonds or double bonds?
What would happen in the case of a diatomic molecule of
nitrogen? Nitrogen has the atomic number 7. What would be
its electronic configuration and its combining capacity? In
order to attain an octet, each nitrogen atom in a molecule of
nitrogen contributes three electrons giving rise to three shared
pairs of electrons. This is said to constitute a triple bond
between the two atoms. The electron dot structure of N2 and
its triple bond can be depicted as in Fig. 4.4.
A molecule of ammonia has the formula NH3. Can you draw
the electron dot structure for this molecule showing how all
four atoms achieve noble gas configuration? Will the molecule
have single, double or triple bonds?
Let us now take a look at methane, which is a compound
of carbon. Methane is widely used as a fuel and is a major
component of bio-gas and Compressed Natural Gas (CNG). It
is also one of the simplest compounds formed by carbon.
Methane has a formula CH4. Hydrogen, as you know, has a
valency of 1. Carbon is tetravalent because it has four valence
electrons. In order to achieve noble gas configuration, carbon
shares these electrons with four atoms of hydrogen as shown
in Fig. 4.5.
Such bonds which are formed by the sharing of an electron pair
between two atoms are known as covalent bonds. Covalently bonded
molecules are seen to have strong bonds within the molecule, but inter-
molecular forces are weak. This gives rise to the low melting and boiling

Allotropes of carbon
The element carbon occurs in different forms in nature with
widely varying physical properties. Both diamond and
graphite are formed by carbon atoms, the difference lies in
the manner in which the carbon atoms are bonded to one
another. In diamond, each carbon atom is bonded to four
other carbon atoms forming a rigid three-dimensional
structure. In graphite, each carbon atom is bonded to three
other carbon atoms in the same plane giving a hexagonal array.
One of these bonds is a double-bond, and thus the valency of
carbon is satisfied. Graphite structure is formed by the
hexagonal arrays being placed in layers one above the other.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's start by remembering what we learned about ionic compounds. They have high melting and boiling points, and they conduct electricity when dissolved in water or melted. Now we're going to look at carbon compounds, and right away we notice they behave very differently. If you look at a table of carbon compounds like acetic acid, chloroform, ethanol, and methane, you'll see their melting and boiling points are quite low compared to ionic compounds. They're also poor conductors of electricity. So what does that tell us? It tells us two things. First, the forces holding these molecules together aren't very strong. Second, because they don't conduct electricity, there are no ions being formed. So whatever kind of bonding carbon uses, it isn't the ionic kind.

Now let's think about carbon itself. Its atomic number is six, so it has four electrons in its outermost shell. To reach a stable, full outer shell like a noble gas, it would need to either gain four electrons or lose four electrons. But both of those are really hard. Gaining four electrons would mean the nucleus, with only six protons, has to hold onto ten electrons. That's a stretch. Losing four electrons would take an enormous amount of energy. So carbon finds a clever way out. Instead of gaining or losing, it shares its electrons with other atoms. When two atoms share a pair of electrons, those shared electrons count toward both atoms' outer shells, so both atoms feel like they have a full shell. This shared pair is called a covalent bond.

Think about hydrogen, the simplest example. Each hydrogen atom has just one electron and needs one more to fill its first shell. Two hydrogen atoms share their electrons, and now each one feels like it has two, just like helium. When atoms share two pairs of electrons, like in oxygen, that's a double bond. When they share three pairs, like in nitrogen, that's a triple bond. Carbon, with four valence electrons, is tetravalent, meaning it shares with four atoms at once, as it does in methane, where carbon shares with four hydrogen atoms. The key idea is that covalent bonds are strong inside the molecule, but the attraction between separate molecules is weak, and that's exactly why these compounds melt and boil at low temperatures and don't conduct electricity.

events.text: Gaining or losing 4 electrons needs too much energy — impossible
Q: What do the melting and boiling points of carbon compounds reveal about their intermolecular forces?
Acetic acid: melts 290 K, boils 391 K
Chloroform: melts 209 K, boils 334 K
Ethanol: melts 156 K, boils 351 K
Methane: melts 90 K, boils 111 K
These values are low compared to ionic compounds, so the forces between carbon-compound molecules are weak.
Q: Why can't carbon simply gain or lose four electrons?
Option 1 — Gain 4 electrons: forms C4- with 10 electrons, but 6 protons can't hold 10 electrons
Option 2 — Lose 4 electrons: forms C4+ with 2 electrons, but removing 4 electrons needs too much energy
Carbon shares electrons rather than gaining or losing four
Q: How do two hydrogen atoms bond to form H2?
Hydrogen, atomic number 1, has 1 electron in K shell and needs 1 more.
Two H atoms each share one electron to form H2.
H2 forms by one shared pair = one single covalent bond; each H attains helium's stable 2-electron K shell.
Q: How do two oxygen atoms bond to complete their octets?
Each oxygen has 6 electrons in L shell, needs 2 more
Each oxygen shares 2 electrons with the other
Two shared pairs = a double bond between the two oxygen atoms
Q: How does a diatomic nitrogen molecule bond?
Each nitrogen contributes three electrons to attain an octet
Three shared pairs of electrons form a triple bond between the two nitrogen atoms
Q: How does carbon bond with hydrogen to form methane (CH4)?
Hydrogen valency = 1; Carbon has 4 valence electrons (tetravalent)
Carbon shares its 4 electrons, one with each of 4 hydrogen atoms
Methane (CH4): carbon shares its 4 electrons with 4 hydrogen atoms, forming 4 covalent bonds
Shared pair = one covalent bond

Carbon is tetravalent because it has four valence electrons. <<WRITE_STEP:Hydrogen valency = 1; Carbon has 4 valence electrons (tetravalent)|id=ex-step-1-1>> In order to achieve a noble gas configuration, carbon shares these electrons with four atoms of hydrogen. 4.2 VERSATILE NATURE OF CARBON
We have seen the formation of covalent bonds by the sharing of
electrons in various elements and compounds. We have also seen the
structure of a simple carbon compound, methane. In the beginning
of the Chapter, we saw how many things we use contain carbon. In
fact, we ourselves are made up of carbon compounds. The numbers
of carbon compounds whose formulae are known to chemists was
recently estimated to be in millions! This outnumbers by a large
margin the compounds formed by all the other elements put together.
Why is it that this property is seen in carbon and no other element?
The nature of the covalent bond enables carbon to form a large number
of compounds. Two factors noticed in the case of carbon are –
(i)
Carbon has the unique ability to form bonds with other atoms of
carbon, giving rise to large molecules. This property is called
catenation. These compounds may have long chains of carbon,
branched chains of carbon or even carbon atoms arranged in rings.
In addition, carbon atoms may be linked by single, double or triple
bonds. Compounds of carbon, which are linked by only single
bonds between the carbon atoms are called saturated compounds.
Compounds of carbon having double or triple bonds between their
carbon atoms are called unsaturated compounds.
No other element exhibits the property of catenation to the extent
seen in carbon compounds. Silicon forms compounds with
hydrogen which have chains of upto seven or eight atoms, but these
compounds are very reactive. The carbon-carbon bond is very strong
and hence stable. This gives us the large number of compounds
with many carbon atoms linked to each other.
(ii)
Since carbon has a valency of four, it is capable of bonding with
four other atoms of carbon or atoms of some other mono-valent
element. Compounds of carbon are formed with oxygen, hydrogen,
nitrogen, sulphur, chlorine and many other elements giving rise to
compounds with specific properties which depend on the elements
other than carbon present in the molecule.
Again the bonds that carbon forms with most other elements are
very strong making these compounds exceptionally stable. One
reason for the formation of strong bonds by carbon is its small size.
This enables the nucleus to hold on to the shared pairs of electrons
strongly. The bonds formed by elements having bigger atoms are
much weaker.
Reprint 2026-27

Carbon and its Compounds
63
Organic compounds
The two characteristic features seen in carbon, that is, tetravalency and catenation, put
together give rise to a large number of compounds. Many have the same non-carbon
atom or group of atoms attached to different carbon chains. These compounds were
initially extracted from natural substances and it was thought that these carbon
compounds or organic compounds could only be formed within a living system. That is,
it was postulated that a ‘vital force’ was necessary for their synthesis. Friedrich Wöhler
disproved this in 1828 by preparing urea from ammonium cyanate. But carbon
compounds, except for carbides, oxides of carbon, carbonate and hydrogencarbonate
salts continue to be studied under organic chemistry.
topics.our_understanding:
Let's think about why carbon is such a superstar among all the elements. Chemists have counted the carbon compounds they know about, and the number runs into the millions. That's more than all the compounds made by every other element put together! So what makes carbon so special? It comes down to two key features, both connected to the way carbon forms covalent bonds by sharing electrons.

The first feature is something called catenation. This is carbon's amazing ability to bond with other carbon atoms, building up large molecules. Imagine carbon atoms linking hands to form long chains, or chains that branch off in different directions, or even joining up into rings. And the links between them can be single bonds, double bonds, or even triple bonds. When carbon atoms are joined only by single bonds, we call those saturated compounds. When there are double or triple bonds in there, we call them unsaturated compounds. Now, other elements can't really do this the way carbon can. Silicon, for example, can form chains with hydrogen, but only up to about seven or eight atoms, and those compounds are very reactive and fall apart easily. The carbon-carbon bond, on the other hand, is very strong and stable, so carbon can build enormous structures.

The second feature is carbon's valency of four. Carbon has four electrons to share, so it can bond with four other atoms at once. These can be more carbon atoms, or atoms of other elements like oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen, sulphur, chlorine and many more. Each different element brings its own special properties to the compound. And here's a nice detail: the reason carbon forms such strong bonds is its small size. Because the carbon atom is small, its nucleus can hold tightly onto the shared electrons. Bigger atoms hold their shared electrons more loosely, so their bonds are weaker.

There's a lovely bit of history here too. Compounds of carbon were once called organic compounds because people believed they could only be made inside living things, thanks to some mysterious 'vital force.' But in eighteen twenty-eight, a scientist named Friedrich Wohler proved this wrong by making urea, a compound found in living bodies, from ammonium cyanate in the lab. So tetravalency and catenation together are the secret to carbon's incredible variety.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's build up carbon compounds step by step, just like assembling something with building blocks. You already know methane, which is one carbon joined to four hydrogens. Now let's meet ethane, whose formula is two carbons and six hydrogens. Here's the trick for drawing these structures. First, you link the carbon atoms together with a single bond. So you draw carbon joined to carbon. Now think about valency. Carbon has a valency of four, meaning it wants to form four bonds. When the two carbons hold hands with one bond, each carbon has used up only one of its four bonds. That leaves three unsatisfied bonds on each carbon. So the second step is to fill those gaps with hydrogen. You attach three hydrogens to each carbon, and now everybody is happy. Every atom has all its bonds satisfied. You can try this yourself with propane, which has three carbons and eight hydrogens. Link the carbons in a chain, then add hydrogens until every valency is filled. When all the bonds in a compound are single bonds and every valency is satisfied this way, we call it a saturated compound. Saturated compounds are normally not very reactive, because they're already comfortable and complete.

Now here's where it gets interesting. There's another compound called ethene, with two carbons and four hydrogens. Notice it has fewer hydrogens than ethane. Try the same steps. Link the two carbons with a single bond, then add hydrogens. But you'll find that this time, after placing the hydrogens, one bond on each carbon is still left unsatisfied. There simply aren't enough hydrogens to go around. How do we fix this? The two carbons form a second bond between themselves, creating a double bond. Now everyone's valency is satisfied. There's an even more extreme example called ethyne, with two carbons and only two hydrogens. Here the carbons need a triple bond between them to satisfy their valencies. Compounds like ethene and ethyne, which have double or triple bonds between carbon atoms, are called unsaturated compounds. And here's the key insight: these unsaturated compounds are more reactive than saturated ones. Those extra bonds are like coiled springs, eager to react and rearrange. So just by counting hydrogens, you can tell whether a carbon compound is calm and saturated or lively and unsaturated.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's build on what we already know. Earlier we met methane, ethane, and propane, which have one, two, and three carbon atoms. Here's the wonderful thing about carbon: those chains of carbon atoms can keep growing. Add a fourth carbon and you get butane, a fifth gives pentane, and a sixth gives hexane. Each carbon links to the next, like beads on a string, and the leftover bonds get filled up with hydrogen atoms. These chains, where every carbon is connected by single bonds and is holding as many hydrogens as it can, are called saturated compounds.

Now here's where it gets really interesting. Take butane, with four carbon atoms. You might think there's only one way to arrange four carbons, but there are actually two. You can line all four up in a straight row, or you can take three in a row and stick the fourth one out to the side as a branch. Both arrangements end up with the same formula: four carbons and ten hydrogens. Same formula, but a different shape, a different structure. Compounds like this, with an identical molecular formula but different structures, are called structural isomers. This is a big idea, because it means one formula can describe more than one actual molecule.

Carbon doesn't stop at straight and branched chains either. Sometimes the carbon atoms join up into a ring, with the two ends of the chain connecting back to each other. Cyclohexane is a good example. It has the formula six carbons and twelve hydrogens, arranged in a six-carbon ring. Try drawing the electron dot structure for it yourself, just to test your understanding.

Straight chains, branched chains, and rings can all be saturated or unsaturated. Remember, unsaturated means there's at least one double or triple bond between carbon atoms. Benzene is a famous ring compound that's unsaturated, with the formula six carbons and six hydrogens.

Finally, let's give these families their proper names. Any compound made of only carbon and hydrogen is called a hydrocarbon. Among hydrocarbons, the saturated ones, with only single bonds, are called alkanes. The unsaturated ones with one or more double bonds are alkenes, and those with one or more triple bonds are alkynes. So with just a few naming rules, you can sort a huge variety of carbon compounds into neat groups.

topics.our_understanding:
Up to now, we've been thinking about carbon as an element that happily bonds with hydrogen, making those chains and rings we call hydrocarbons. But here's the lovely thing about carbon — it's a very friendly element. It doesn't only make friends with hydrogen. Carbon can also form bonds with other elements like the halogens, which are chlorine, bromine, fluorine, and iodine, as well as oxygen, nitrogen, and sulphur. So our picture of carbon compounds suddenly gets much richer.

Now think about a hydrocarbon chain. It has carbon atoms linked together, with hydrogen atoms hanging off the spare bonds. What if we take one of those hydrogen atoms and swap it out, replacing it with one of these other elements? As long as we do this carefully so that carbon's valency — its bonding capacity of four — stays satisfied, the molecule is perfectly happy. When an element comes in to replace a hydrogen like this, we give it a special name: a heteroatom. The word just means a different kind of atom that has taken hydrogen's place.

Sometimes it isn't a single atom that replaces the hydrogen, but a whole little cluster or group of atoms. And here is the key insight: these heteroatoms, and the groups that contain them, give the compound its own special character. Think of it this way — no matter how long the carbon chain is, no matter whether it's straight or branched, the presence of one of these groups decides how the compound behaves and reacts. Because they determine the function, the behaviour, of the compound, we call them functional groups.

This is a really powerful idea. It means that if you know what functional group a molecule has, you already know a lot about how it will act, regardless of the rest of the molecule. Chemists organise the world of carbon compounds around these functional groups. In a table of these groups, you'll often see a single line drawn coming off the group. That single line represents a free valency — the spot where the group attaches to the carbon chain by taking the place of a hydrogen atom. So whenever you see that little dangling line, just picture it reaching out and hooking onto the carbon skeleton where a hydrogen used to be. That simple swap is what opens the door to the huge variety of carbon compounds we'll meet.

You have seen that carbon atoms can be linked together to form chains

hydrogen atom or other atoms on these carbon chains can be replaced

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about something that brings a beautiful order to the messy world of carbon compounds. You already know that carbon atoms can link up into chains of different lengths, and those chains can have branches, and that hydrogen atoms on those chains can be swapped out for functional groups like the alcohol group. Here's the key insight: when a compound has a particular functional group, that group decides how the compound behaves chemically, no matter how long the carbon chain is. So if you take methanol, then ethanol, then propanol, then butanol, all of them have that alcohol group, and so they all react in very similar ways. A family of compounds like this, where the same functional group sits on carbon chains of increasing length, is called a homologous series.

Now here's the neat pattern. If you line up the members of a series and look at how each one differs from the next, you'll find they always differ by the same little unit, a carbon plus two hydrogens, what we call a CH2 unit. Take methane and ethane, they differ by one CH2 unit. Ethane and propane, again one CH2 unit. Each step up the ladder just adds one more CH2. Because of this steady pattern, we can write a single general formula that captures every member. For alkenes, that formula is C n H two n, where n can be two, three, four, and so on. You can play the same game to find general formulas for alkanes and alkynes.

And there's one more lovely thing. As you climb the series and the molecular mass increases, the physical properties change in a smooth, gradual way. Melting points and boiling points rise steadily, and things like solubility shift in a regular fashion too. But the chemical properties, which depend only on the functional group, stay basically the same throughout the family. So a homologous series gives you predictability, change in physical properties, sameness in chemical behavior. That's why chemists love it.

4.2.5 Nomenclature of Carbon Compounds
The names of compounds in a homologous series are based on the name
of the basic carbon chain modified by a “prefix” “phrase before” or “suffix”
“phrase after” indicating the nature of the functional group. For example,
the names of the alcohols taken in Activity 4.2 are methanol, ethanol,
propanol and butanol.
Naming a carbon compound can be done by the following method –
(i)
Identify the number of carbon atoms in the compound. A compound
having three carbon atoms would have the name propane.
(ii)
In case a functional group is present, it is indicated in the
name of the compound with either a prefix or a suffix (as given
in Table 4.4).
(iii)
If the name of the functional group is to be given as a suffix, and the
suffix of the functional group begins with a vowel a, e, i, o, u, then
the name of the carbon chain is modified by deleting the final ‘e’ and
adding the appropriate suffix. For example, a three-carbon chain
with a ketone group would be named in the following manner –
Propane – ‘e’ = propan + ‘one’ = propanone.
(iv)
If the carbon chain is unsaturated, then the final ‘ane’ in the name
of the carbon chain is substituted by ‘ene’ or ‘yne’ as given in
Table 4.4. For example, a three-carbon chain with a double bond
would be called propene and if it has a triple bond, it would be
called propyne.

In this section we learn how chemists give names to carbon compounds. Think of it like a system of rules, so that anyone in the world can hear a name and know exactly what molecule you mean. The whole idea rests on two parts: the basic carbon chain, and the functional group attached to it. We use a prefix, which is a phrase that comes before, or a suffix, which is a phrase that comes after, to tell which functional group is present.

The first step is always to count the carbon atoms. A compound with three carbon atoms is built on the name propane. One carbon gives methane, two gives ethane, four gives butane, and so on. That part of the name is fixed by the number of carbons.

Next, if there is a functional group, we show it in the name. Sometimes it goes in front, like the prefix chloro or bromo for the halogens. Other times it goes at the end as a suffix, such as ol for alcohols, al for aldehydes, one for ketones, and oic acid for carboxylic acids.

Now here is a small but important rule. When the suffix begins with a vowel, meaning a, e, i, o, or u, we drop the final letter e from the carbon chain name before adding the suffix. So for a three carbon chain with a ketone group, we take propane, remove the e to get propan, and add one. That gives us propanone. Notice how smoothly the name flows once the e is gone.

Finally, we deal with whether the chain is saturated or unsaturated. If every bond is a single bond, the name ends in ane. But if there is a double bond, we replace ane with ene, giving propene for a three carbon chain. And if there is a triple bond, we replace ane with yne, giving propyne. So just by reading the ending of a name, you can tell whether the molecule has only single bonds, a double bond, or a triple bond. Once you practice this, naming any simple carbon compound becomes a neat, logical puzzle rather than something to memorize blindly.

4.3 CHEMICAL PROPERTIES OF CARBON COMPOUNDS
In this section we will be studying about some of the chemical properties
of carbon compounds. Since most of the fuels we use are either carbon
or its compounds, we shall first study combustion.
topics.our_understanding:
Let's start thinking about what carbon compounds actually do when they react. Up to now, you've been learning about how carbon atoms join together and form all sorts of structures, like long chains and rings, and how they bond with other elements. But knowing how a molecule is built is only half the story. The other half, the really exciting half, is what these compounds do when they take part in chemical reactions. That's what we call their chemical properties.

Now, here's a thought worth holding onto. Almost every fuel you can name burns to give you energy. Think about the wood in a campfire, the coal in a power station, the petrol or diesel in a car, the natural gas in a kitchen stove, even the candle on a birthday cake. What do all of these have in common? They are either carbon itself or compounds that contain carbon. That's a remarkable pattern, and it's no accident. Carbon and its compounds are the workhorses that power so much of our daily lives.

Because of this, the very first chemical property we're going to look at is combustion, which is just the scientific word for burning. When a carbon compound burns, it reacts with oxygen from the air, and in that reaction it releases heat and usually light too. That release of energy is exactly why we use these substances as fuels in the first place.

So as we move forward, keep this big idea in your mind. We're not just memorizing reactions for the sake of it. We're discovering why carbon compounds matter so much to us, and combustion is our doorway into that understanding. After we explore burning, we'll go on to look at other ways carbon compounds react and change. But for now, just appreciate that the section ahead is really about how carbon compounds behave, and why their behavior, starting with the way they burn, is so deeply tied to the energy that keeps our world running.

events.text: Combustion = reacting with oxygen, releasing energy
Fuel + plenty of oxygen gives carbon dioxide + water + energy
Blue flame = complete combustion

topics.standalone_narration_text: Every flame you have ever seen — a candle, a gas stove, a forest fire — is carbon coming apart and handing its energy to the world. Up to now you have learned how carbon atoms join into chains and rings. But building a molecule is only half the story — the exciting half is what these molecules DO when they react. <<SECTION:Chemical Properties of Carbon Compounds|id=sec-1>> And the single most important thing carbon compounds do is burn. We call this combustion, and it is the chemical property behind almost every fuel on Earth. <<PAUSE:short>> Here is what burning really is: a carbon compound grabs oxygen from the air, locks onto it tightly, and in doing so it spills out its stored energy as heat and light. <<WRITE_TEXT:Combustion = reacting with oxygen, releasing energy|id=text-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> When carbon meets enough oxygen, it joins with it completely to make carbon dioxide, and the leftover energy escapes as heat and light. <<WRITE_EQUATION:C + O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + \text{heat} + \text{light}|id=eq-1|boxed>> So when pure carbon meets plenty of oxygen, it combines completely to form carbon dioxide, and the energy left over rushes off as heat and light. But does it always burn this cleanly? What happens if there is not enough oxygen to go around? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Watch a fuel like methane: with enough oxygen it burns fully, giving carbon dioxide and water, and a clean burst of energy. <<WRITE_STEP:Fuel + plenty of oxygen gives carbon dioxide + water + energy|id=step-1>> A fuel like methane burns by combining with oxygen to give carbon dioxide and water, releasing a burst of energy. <<WRITE_EQUATION:CH_4 + 2O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + 2H_2O + \text{energy}|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<FOCUS:blue-flame>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:carbon_and_its_compounds:4_3:flame_comparison>> Now look at the board. On the left, a burner with plenty of air flowing in — see how the flame is small, steady, and blue. <<POINT:blue-flame>> <<FOCUS:oxygen-arrows-blue>> Those inward arrows are oxygen pouring in. With this much oxygen, every carbon atom finds a partner and burns completely. That clean blue flame is the signature of complete combustion. <<WRITE_KEY:Blue flame = complete combustion|id=key-1>> <<POINT:oxygen-arrows-blue>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:yellow-flame>> Now starve the same flame of air. With only a few arrows of oxygen, the flame turns tall, yellow, and flickering. <<POINT:yellow-flame>> <<FOCUS:soot-particles>> There is not enough oxygen for every carbon atom, so some carbon escapes unburnt — these black specks are soot. A smoky yellow flame is the signature of incomplete combustion. <<POINT:soot-particles>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> So next time you see a flame, read it like a chemist: combustion is carbon compounds meeting oxygen to release heat and light, and the colour tells you whether that meeting was complete or starved of air. <<PAUSE:short>>

various biological and geological processes. Coal is the remains of trees, ferns, and

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about combustion, which is just a fancy word for burning. Here's the big idea: carbon, in every form it comes in, burns in oxygen to give us carbon dioxide, and along with that, it releases heat and light. Most carbon compounds do the same thing. When you burn them, they give off lots of heat and light. These are oxidation reactions, the kind where something combines with oxygen.

Think about three simple cases. When pure carbon burns in oxygen, it gives carbon dioxide plus heat and light. When methane burns, it gives carbon dioxide, water, plus heat and light. And when ethanol, which is alcohol, burns, it also gives carbon dioxide, water, plus heat and light. Notice the pattern. Carbon ends up as carbon dioxide and the hydrogen ends up as water.

Now here's something practical and interesting. Not all flames look the same. Saturated hydrocarbons, the ones with only single bonds, usually burn with a clean flame. But unsaturated compounds, with double or triple bonds, burn with a yellow flame and lots of black smoke. That black stuff is soot, and soot is really just carbon that didn't fully burn. If you hold a metal plate over such a flame, you'll see a dark deposit on it.

But here's the twist. Even a clean-burning saturated fuel will turn sooty if you limit the air supply. That's called incomplete combustion. When there isn't enough oxygen, the carbon doesn't fully convert to carbon dioxide, so you get soot. This is exactly why your gas stove at home has little air holes at the base. They let in enough oxygen to give a clean blue flame. If you ever notice the bottoms of your cooking pots turning black, that means the air holes are blocked and fuel is being wasted.

There's also a pollution angle. Fuels like coal and petroleum contain some nitrogen and sulphur. When they burn, they form oxides of sulphur and nitrogen, and these are major air pollutants.

Finally, why do some things burn with a flame and others just glow? A flame only appears when gaseous substances burn. A candle or cooking gas burns with a flame because gases are burning. But coal or charcoal in a simple stove often just glows red, giving heat without a flame, because there's no gas burning. The colour you see in a flame comes from heated atoms glowing, and each element gives its own characteristic colour.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about oxidation, which is a really useful idea when we're working with carbon compounds. You already met oxidation back in an earlier chapter, where it was described as the adding of oxygen to a substance. Carbon compounds love to get oxidised. The most obvious way is combustion, which is simply burning. When carbon compounds burn, they combine completely with oxygen and release a lot of heat. But there's another, gentler kind of oxidation happening in the world of carbon, and that's what we focus on here.

Think about alcohols, like ethanol. Through a special kind of reaction, an alcohol can be converted into a carboxylic acid. In simple words, we add oxygen to the alcohol, and what comes out is an acid. This is a partial oxidation, not the dramatic burning kind. To make this happen, we need a helper substance that's willing to hand over oxygen to the alcohol. There's a nice experiment to see this in action. You take a small amount of ethanol in a test tube, warm it gently in a water bath, and then add a purple solution called alkaline potassium permanganate, drop by drop.

Here's the interesting part. When you add the first few drops, the purple colour disappears. Why? Because the permanganate is busy doing its job, giving away its oxygen to turn the alcohol into an acid. As long as there's alcohol still waiting to be oxidised, the colour keeps vanishing. But once you've added so much that all the alcohol has already been converted, the extra permanganate has nothing left to react with. So the purple colour stays, and now it doesn't disappear anymore. That moment tells you the reaction is complete.

Notice the key idea hiding inside this experiment. Some substances are capable of adding oxygen to other substances. We give these helpers a special name: oxidising agents. Both alkaline potassium permanganate and acidified potassium dichromate are examples of oxidising agents, because they hand oxygen to the alcohol and push it forward into becoming an acid. So whenever you hear the words oxidising agent, just remember it's the substance that supplies the oxygen and makes the oxidation happen. This concept matters because oxidation reactions are everywhere in chemistry, and being able to turn one type of compound into another, like an alcohol into an acid, is exactly the kind of control chemists need.

topics.orig_book_content:
4.3.3 Addition Reaction
Unsaturated hydrocarbons add hydrogen in the presence of catalysts
such as palladium or nickel to give saturated hydrocarbons. Catalysts
are substances that cause a reaction to occur or proceed at a different
rate without the reaction itself being affected. This reaction is commonly
used in the hydrogenation of vegetable oils using a nickel catalyst.
Vegetable oils generally have long unsaturated carbon chains while
animal fats have saturated carbon chains.
You must have seen advertisements stating that some vegetable oils
are ‘healthy’. Animal fats generally contain saturated fatty acids which
are said to be harmful for health. Oils containing unsaturated fatty acids
should be chosen for cooking.
topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about addition reactions, which are special to unsaturated hydrocarbons. Remember, unsaturated hydrocarbons are the ones with double or triple bonds between carbon atoms. Because they have these extra bonds, they're a bit reactive — they have room to take on more atoms. That's exactly what happens in an addition reaction. When you bring an unsaturated hydrocarbon together with hydrogen, the hydrogen atoms get added across the double or triple bond, and the molecule becomes saturated, meaning all single bonds. So an unsaturated hydrocarbon turns into a saturated one.

But here's the catch — this doesn't happen easily on its own. You need a helper called a catalyst. Common catalysts for this are palladium and nickel. Now, what is a catalyst? Think of it as a substance that helps a reaction happen, or makes it happen faster, but the catalyst itself comes out unchanged at the end. It's like a coach who helps the team play better but doesn't actually run onto the field and score. The reaction speeds up, the catalyst stays the same.

Why does this matter in real life? This is the basis of something called hydrogenation of vegetable oils, and it uses a nickel catalyst. Here's the idea. Vegetable oils generally have long carbon chains that are unsaturated — they've got those double bonds. Animal fats, on the other hand, have saturated carbon chains. When you add hydrogen to a liquid vegetable oil, you saturate it, and it turns into something more solid, like the fats you see in margarine or ghee substitutes.

Now there's a health angle here too. You've probably seen advertisements calling some vegetable oils 'healthy.' Animal fats generally contain saturated fatty acids, and these are said to be harmful for our health. Oils with unsaturated fatty acids are considered the better choice for cooking. So when you understand addition reactions, you also understand why turning unsaturated oils into saturated fats — through hydrogenation — changes both their physical state and their effect on health. Notice how one small chemistry idea, adding hydrogen across a double bond, connects all the way to the food on your plate. That's the beauty of this topic.

4.3.4 Substitution Reaction
Saturated hydrocarbons are fairly unreactive and are inert in the presence
of most reagents. However, in the presence of sunlight, chlorine is added
to hydrocarbons in a very fast reaction. Chlorine can replace the hydrogen
atoms one by one. It is called a substitution reaction because one type
of atom or a group of atoms takes the place of another. A number of
products are usually formed with the higher homologues of alkanes.
CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl (in the presence of sunlight)

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about saturated hydrocarbons, those carbon compounds where every bond is a single bond, like the alkanes. The first thing you should know is that these molecules are fairly lazy. We call them unreactive, or inert, which means they don't easily react with most chemicals you throw at them. So how do you get a calm, stable molecule to do something interesting? You need a special trigger, and here that trigger is sunlight.

Imagine you have methane, the simplest hydrocarbon, sitting with some chlorine gas. In the dark, not much happens. But the moment you shine sunlight on this mixture, a very fast reaction kicks off. The chlorine starts attacking the methane and replaces the hydrogen atoms one by one. Picture the methane molecule as a central carbon holding four hydrogen atoms. A chlorine atom comes in, kicks out one hydrogen, and takes its own place there. The hydrogen that got removed doesn't just float away alone, it joins another chlorine to form hydrogen chloride.

This kind of reaction has a special name, the substitution reaction. The word substitution should remind you of a substitute in a sports game, where one player takes the place of another. Here, one type of atom or group of atoms takes the place of another atom. In our example, chlorine substitutes for hydrogen.

Now here's an important detail. With methane, you might get one neat product. But with the bigger members of the alkane family, the higher homologues, you usually end up with a whole mixture of products. Why? Because chlorine can replace the hydrogens one after another, so you can get a molecule with one chlorine, or two chlorines, or three, and so on. That gives you several different products all at once.

The key reaction to remember is this: methane reacts with chlorine, in the presence of sunlight, to give chloromethane plus hydrogen chloride. Notice that one hydrogen on the methane has been swapped out for a chlorine atom, and the leftover hydrogen leaves combined with chlorine. That single swap is the heart of what substitution means. So the big takeaways are simple: saturated hydrocarbons are unreactive, sunlight makes them react with chlorine, and the reaction works by substituting hydrogen atoms with chlorine, often producing a mixture when the molecules are larger.

topics.orig_book_content:
4.4 SOME IMPORTANT CARBON COMPOUNDS – ETHANOL
AND ETHANOIC ACID
Many carbon compounds are invaluable to us. But here we shall study
the properties of two commercially important compounds – ethanol and
ethanoic acid.
Reprint 2026-27

Science
72
topics.our_understanding:
This little section is really just a doorway into something bigger, so let me set the scene for you. By now you've learned that carbon is special. It forms an enormous number of compounds because each carbon atom can link up with four other atoms, and it can even bond to other carbon atoms to make long chains, branched chains, and rings. That ability gives us millions of different carbon compounds, and many of them are incredibly useful in our daily lives. Think about the fuels we burn, the plastics we use, the medicines we take, and the food we eat. A huge fraction of all of that is built from carbon.

Now, you can't study every single carbon compound, there are simply too many. So what chemists do, and what this section invites you to do, is pick a couple of really important examples and study them carefully. Once you understand how one or two compounds behave, you start to see patterns that apply to whole families of similar compounds. That's the smart way to learn chemistry, learn the representative members deeply rather than memorizing endless lists.

The two compounds chosen here are ethanol and ethanoic acid. Why these two? Because they are commercially important, meaning they matter a lot in industry and in everyday life. Ethanol is the alcohol found in alcoholic drinks, but it's also used as a solvent, in medicines like tinctures and cough syrups, and as a fuel. Ethanoic acid is the acid that gives vinegar its sour taste and sharp smell, and it's widely used in preserving food and in making other chemicals.

So as we move forward, keep in mind the goal. We are going to look at the properties of ethanol and ethanoic acid, how they look, how they smell, how they dissolve, and most importantly how they react with other substances. Notice that we're not picking these compounds randomly. They both have only two carbon atoms, they're both simple enough to understand, and yet they show off the typical behavior of two big families, the alcohols and the carboxylic acids. Learning them well is like getting a master key that opens up an understanding of many related compounds. That's the spirit of this section, it's a promise of useful chemistry to come.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's get to know ethanol, which most people simply call alcohol. At room temperature, ethanol is a liquid, and it's the ingredient that makes alcoholic drinks alcoholic. One of its most useful traits is that it's a great solvent, meaning many substances dissolve well in it. That's why we find ethanol in medicines like tincture iodine, in cough syrups, and in many tonics. It also mixes with water in any proportion you like, which is unusual and handy. Now, a serious word about health. Drinking small amounts of dilute ethanol causes drunkenness, and while this is a widespread social habit, it's harmful and discouraged. Pure ethanol, called absolute alcohol, can actually kill you even in small amounts, and drinking alcohol over a long time leads to many health problems.

Now let's look at how ethanol reacts, because that tells us about its chemistry. First, ethanol reacts with sodium metal. When you drop a small piece of sodium into ethanol, hydrogen gas bubbles off, and the other product is a compound called sodium ethoxide. This is a useful clue: it reminds us that metals reacting with certain substances release hydrogen, just like metals reacting with acids do.

The second important reaction turns ethanol into an unsaturated hydrocarbon. If you heat ethanol to about four hundred forty-three kelvin with excess concentrated sulphuric acid, the ethanol loses water and becomes ethene, which has a double bond. Here the concentrated sulphuric acid acts as a dehydrating agent, meaning it pulls water out of the ethanol molecule.

There's also a fascinating side note worth remembering. Methanol, which looks chemically similar to ethanol, is deadly even in tiny amounts. In the liver, methanol turns into methanal, which reacts quickly with cell components and coagulates the protoplasm, much like cooking coagulates an egg. It also damages the optic nerve and can cause blindness. Because ethanol made for industry shouldn't be drunk, manufacturers add poisons like methanol and blue dye to it. This poisoned, coloured ethanol is called denatured alcohol, and it keeps people from misusing industrial alcohol.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's get to know ethanoic acid, which most people call by its everyday name, acetic acid. It belongs to a family of acids called carboxylic acids. When you dilute acetic acid in water to about five to eight percent, you get vinegar, the sour liquid used to preserve pickles. Here's a fun detail: pure ethanoic acid freezes at two hundred ninety kelvin, which is just a little below room temperature. So in cold climates during winter, it actually turns into ice-like crystals. That's why it earned the nickname glacial acetic acid, because it looks like glaciers.

Now, the most important thing about carboxylic acids is that they are acidic, but they are weak acids. Compare this to a mineral acid like hydrochloric acid, which is fully ionised in water, meaning almost all of its molecules break apart to release hydrogen ions. Ethanoic acid only partly ionises, so even at the same concentration it produces fewer hydrogen ions. That's why if you test both with a universal indicator, hydrochloric acid shows up as the stronger acid. Both will still turn blue litmus red, because both are genuinely acids, but they differ in strength.

Now let's look at how ethanoic acid reacts. First, the esterification reaction. When ethanoic acid reacts with absolute ethanol in the presence of a small amount of concentrated sulphuric acid, which acts as a catalyst, it forms an ester. Esters are sweet-smelling substances, which is why they're used in perfumes and as flavourings. And here's a neat reverse trick: if you treat that ester with sodium hydroxide, an alkali, it turns back into an alcohol and the sodium salt of the carboxylic acid. This reaction is called saponification, because it's how soap is made. Soaps are simply sodium or potassium salts of long-chain carboxylic acids.

Second, ethanoic acid reacts with a base. Just like mineral acids do, it reacts with sodium hydroxide to give a salt called sodium ethanoate, or sodium acetate, plus water.

Third, it reacts with carbonates and hydrogencarbonates. When you add ethanoic acid to sodium carbonate or sodium hydrogencarbonate, you get a salt, water, and carbon dioxide gas bubbling out. You can confirm that gas is carbon dioxide by passing it through limewater, which turns milky. This bubbling test is actually a handy way to tell a carboxylic acid apart from an alcohol, because alcohol won't fizz with these carbonates.

This activity demonstrates the effect of soap in cleaning. Most dirt is
oily in nature and as you know, oil does not dissolve in water. The
molecules of soap are sodium or potassium salts of long-chain carboxylic
acids. The ionic-end of soap interacts with water while the carbon chain
interacts with oil. The soap molecules, thus form structures called
micelles (see Fig. 4.12) where one end of the molecules is towards the oil
droplet while the ionic-end faces outside. This forms an emulsion in
water. The soap micelle thus helps  in pulling out the dirt in water and
we can wash our clothes clean (Fig. 4.13).
Can you draw the structure of the micelle that would be formed if
you dissolve soap in a hydrocarbon?
Micelles
Soaps are molecules in which the two ends have differing properties, one is hydrophilic,
that is, it interacts with water, while the other end is hydrophobic, that is, it interacts
with hydrocarbons. When soap is at the surface of water, the hydrophobic ‘tail’ of soap
will not be soluble in water and the soap will align along the surface of water with the
ionic end in water and the hydrocarbon ‘tail’ protruding out of water. Inside water,
these molecules have a unique orientation that keeps
the hydrocarbon portion out of the water. Thus,
clusters of molecules in which the hydrophobic tails
are in the interior of the cluster and the ionic ends
are on the surface of the cluster. This formation is
called a micelle. Soap in the form of a micelle is able
to clean, since the oily dirt will be collected in the
centre of the micelle. The micelles stay in solution as
a colloid and will not come together to precipitate
because of ion-ion repulsion. Thus, the dirt
suspended in the micelles is also easily rinsed away.
The soap micelles are large enough to scatter light.
Hence a soap solution appears cloudy.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about how soaps and detergents actually clean things, because the chemistry here is really clever. Think about a greasy plate or a dirty shirt. Most dirt that sticks to our clothes and skin is oily in nature. And here's the problem: oil and water just don't mix. You can shake them together as hard as you like, but the oil always comes back together and floats away from the water. So plain water alone can't wash away oily grime.

This is where soap comes in. A soap molecule is a special long molecule that is the sodium or potassium salt of a long-chain carboxylic acid. What makes it so useful is that its two ends behave completely differently. One end is the ionic end, and it loves water — we call it the water-loving, or hydrophilic, end. The other end is a long carbon chain, and it hates water but loves oil and grease — we call it the water-fearing, or hydrophobic, tail. So one molecule has a foot in both worlds.

Now imagine many of these molecules in water with a drop of oil. The oil-loving tails all bury themselves into the oil droplet, while the water-loving ends point outward into the water. They arrange themselves into a little ball called a micelle, with the oily dirt trapped right in the center. This is the heart of how soap works — it grabs the oily dirt and surrounds it. These micelles float around as a colloid and don't clump together, because their charged outer ends repel each other. So the dirt stays suspended and rinses away easily. By the way, these micelles are big enough to scatter light, which is why soapy water looks cloudy.

But soap has a weakness. In hard water — water containing calcium and magnesium salts — soap reacts with those salts and forms an insoluble grayish solid called scum. You've probably noticed foam forming with difficulty and a sticky residue left behind. That wastes soap. To fix this, we use detergents instead. Detergents are usually sodium salts of sulphonic acids, and their charged ends do not form insoluble precipitates with calcium and magnesium. So detergents keep working even in hard water, which is why they're used in shampoos and washing products.

events.text: Head = ionic, water-loving; tail = carbon chain, oil-loving
Soap surrounds oil: tails in, heads out = a micelle
Detergents work the same way; clean even in hard water

questions.q_text: Carbon compounds are generally poor conductors of electricity. What does this tell us about their bonding?
options: A. They form strong ionic bonds
B. They do not form ions

D. They dissolve easily in water

questions.q_text: Why does carbon share electrons rather than gain or lose four electrons?
options: A. Sharing produces ions more easily
B. Gaining or losing four electrons would require too much energy or be very difficult
C. Carbon has no electrons in its outer shell
D. Sharing makes carbon a metal

questions.q_text: When two atoms share three pairs of electrons, what kind of bond is formed?
options: A. A single bond

questions.q_text: Carbon is described as tetravalent. What does this mean?
options: A. It can form a bond with only one other atom
